text: 100% worth of 5 stars if you substitute in a better waitress; hostess and kitchen staff were excellent! However, our waitress was either new or high or just a ditz, either way, Daddy skimped her tip. First off, how had I not heard about this place prior? Soooooo amazing. Soooooo cute. Soooo what my dad and I were looking for in terms of dinner when the rest of the house abandoned us (I don't cook when it's just us two, rarely do I cook for us plus my brother. My number is 4+.) Anyway, I don't understand why I hadn't heard of this amazing little place. I just googled it, it seems to have completely changed since Joe Bonwich of the Post-Dispatch reviewed it in 2008. It's now BBQ in an adorable, but classy setting. The atmosphere is perfect and the whole place smells of BBQ - but not overwhelmingly so. Hard, dark woods with black accents, clean lines and everything is polished. The food though. Ohmylord. New favorite. All my dad and I could talk about was everyone we wanted to bring there. We started with the Smothered Fries - cut potatoes with some skin on, rib meat, a homemade white cheese sauce topped with more cheese. Sooo good. The cheese sauce was creamy and sharp, the fries had a touch of salt and the meat was smokey, which all balanced in perfect harmony. The St. Louis Style Spare Ribs came in true fashion. Rubbed with a thick dry rub and obviously smokey for hours, the meat pulled away from the bone without struggle - literally a baby could have gummed the meet from the bones. The spice rub was great, coated well. My dad had the pulled pork and raved about it. He also tried all three sauces on the table - he couldn't pick his favorite though, all were good. Dessert. Ooooh a sweet ending. They don't have a dessert menu because the head chef's mother does all the baking so the options switch nearly weekly - adorable. We spilt the gooeybutter topped brownie, which is served warm with a glass a milk. Once again, just sooo good. Most def! going back soon. Everything was really good, minus that waitress.

text: Our office came here for our annual Christmas luncheon, which is usually a pretty nice affair. The person coordinating it had a 'good experience' at Terrace View, and I trust her opinion, so I was excited about eating here. Wrong. From the rickety tables and chairs to the concrete floors to the hey-you're-still-in-a-park (it's within Citygarden) 'industrial' restrooms to the waiter detritus everywhere, Terrace View isn't the most comfortable place to eat. I tried to ignore that and ordered an iced tea while staring at the interesting Adam & Eve sculpture in front of me. The lunch menu is pretty short--mostly sandwiches. The server enticed me with the promise of a cayenne-laced carrot soup, so I went for it and the oven-baked mushrooms with goat cheese. Sounds good, right? Wrong. The soup came out looking orange, smooth, and appetizing, but had three distinct flavors: raw carrot followed by watery heat followed by an unpleasant not-quite-sour aftertaste. I put my spoon down after I realized that I was actually forcing myself to eat it. The oven-roasted mushrooms weren't any better. What they call a 'small plate' was really just that: an anemic 5 tablespoons of sliced shiitakes, topped with a few dots of goat cheese. The cheese was warm; the mushrooms were cold. I left hungry. My co-workers ordered sandwiches and almost all of them had something 'off' about them: "The burger was good, BUT way overcooked." "My chicken sandwich was good, BUT the bun was kind of burned." "My eggplant sandwich isn't a sandwich--I need a fork!" The service was fine, but I feel bad for the Terrace View--this place has 'amateur hour, ready to fail' written all over it. Maybe I shouldn't feel bad. A good restaurant should have the opportunity to move into a location with so much potential.

text: I don't ever plan on writing reviews for franchises because essentially, you get the same experience as far as food/drink quality and service goes, especially when the aforementioned franchise is Starbucks. It's kind of impressive and scary how all Starbucks employees (regardless of their make, model, size, shape, sex, skin tone, etc etc) are almost Stepford-ish in how nice, considerate and generally chipper they are. A secret (well not so secret anymore) way to test the general amiability of a Starbucks barista is to walk in, look stupefied, and then say the following words: "I... don't know what to get. Do you have any suggestions?" If they're good, they'll smile and give you some suggestions based on your tastes. If they're great, they'll do the same, but then offer to make you something else for free if you don't like what you bought. This is why I love Starbucks and am annoyed by people who hate it. Yes, they're a big faceless corporation, blah de blah, but they got so big because they make their customers feel like they're the only ones that matter for those brief two minutes. But I'm soapboxing now, so I'll cut it short. This location rocks because I love how it feels like a library with a Starbucks attached. It reminds me of my undergrad days, and even simple things like the bricks in the ceiling, or how there is never a shortage of desks to lay out my books/laptop, or how all of the patrons are considerate and quiet, or even how this location is kind of set a little bit below ground making it feel all... cave-like; all these things just make me love spending time in here. Say hi if you see me. I'm the brown guy with the iDevice headphones on. There aren't many Indians in that location, I mean it's not like there's a really nice private university nearby with Indians all running amok. Oh wait... Ok fine, I'm the Indian guy always wearing flip flops; I know most Indians have an aversion to flip flops.
label: POS

text: WAY Overrated - and this is coming from a carnivore who eats any and every cut of meat. Lured here by every imaginable food critic and magazine, hoping to try real deal Cajun, boy did I leave disappointed. While I understand that they could not prepare a vegetable plate for my vegetarian wife (even though I did my share to support the restaurant by ordering 6 appetizers and 3 entrees for myself), I was dumbfounded by their initial refusal to put on the side, or leave out altogether, the meat toppings (such as fried pigs' ears and fried jerky) from my wife's salads so as not to contaminate her food: "It will confuse the kitchen - you have to understand, this is a busy restaurant." While I'd say that accomodating simple requests and adaptablity are part of what should make a great "James Beard winner" restaurant, I'll take the attitude if the food is good. BUT INSTEAD, Mr. Link could benefit from enrolling in some technique classes, as demonstrated by his: 1) "Spicy" RIBS: I'm texan and my wife is from atlanta, so don't serve me ribs so tough and dry I wonder if the sauce (which tasted store bought) contained Retin-A. By the way, where was the spice?, I could've used it to push down those ribs. 2) Louisiana cochon with turnips, cabbage & cracklins: This was the saltiest, most dried out pork i have ever tried. it was so horrific i took just one bite. The only silver lining is that my friend who demanded I ordered this will be reimbursing me the $22 I spent. PS Donald Link: While I didn't order the crawfish pie, you should know that it looks like an empanada. What came out best here was the Oyster BLT, the Rabbit Livers with Pepper Jelly and the headcheese. So ironically, at a place named "Pig" shy away from pig dishes, particulary those where execution matters, and instead opt for creamier yum-yum food. Cochon gets two stars - while some things were amazing, there were too many *inedible* misses.

text: Awesome place, surprised it has not been reviewed more. I have been a regular for quite some time and Arpeggio has been consistently great. All the food is very tasty, they use top quality ingredients and everything is made in house so nothing has a generic flavor; if for some reason there is something wrong with your food one of the two owners are usually around and more than happy to accommodate you. As mentioned it gets very busy during lunch and weekends/holidays, waits of 1-1.5+hrs are normal; they only take reservations for parties of 6+, so get there early. For the most part the waitresses are all friendly and provide good service, even when it's very busy. The place is small and they pack people in so do not plan on a quiet romantic evening unless you go after 9:30. I have tried just about everything on the menu and all of it really is very good. They serve a mix of pizza, mediterranean fare, and greek, they also have several healthy and vegetarian options. If it's your first time definitely try the hummus or baba and a pizza, you can't go wrong. In general I prefer the cheaper entrees as the fish and meat is slightly overpriced, though it is still very good. It's BYO also so do not forget your own alcohol!

text: On a cold winter's night in between hanging out with some new friends and dinner at a delicious Moroccan restaurant, I was feeling about a beer low, and decided to head into the warmth of the Rathskeller. This place was absolutely PACKED! Lots of friendly faces enjoying what looked like some pretty tasty food. As I made my way back to the Keller bar, I passed quite a few very friendly servers and happy patrons, and was immediately drawn into the size of this place! The Keller bar is huge! Various animal heads on the walls, some cool flags, neat signage, and random kitschy stuff completes the feeling that you're hanging out in a random German bar. There were, however, a few things that made me wish I was actually in a random German bar instead of the Rathskeller... first and foremost, the service was quite indifferent, just like what Emily said. text: Amazing breakfasts? *check* Monster sandwiches and portions? *check* Dr. Browns soda? *check* For a Jewish kid raised around these types of food, when I walk in to Famous and see their long glass cases filled with huge pastries, cakes, followed by smoked fish and deli meats, I can feel it in my heart. No, that's my my heart preparing for the artery clogging goodness that awaits it, that's love that I'm feeling. Famous runs the show for the Jewish deli scene in the Philadelphia area.The closest thing to Famous between here and NYC is Harold's deli in Edison, NJ, though Famous is obviously much closer. Everything at Famous is huge, from the challah french toast, to the bowls of soup, to especially the sandwiches. The sandwiches are easily enough to share (unless you have an endless pit of a stomach like me). Famous is perfect for breakfast, especially on Sundays, then it's the place to be. Ask for a booth "by the windows", which is a line of maybe 15+ booths that run along Bainbridge so you can watch all the action. My personal recommendations: Breakfast: *The traditional challah french toast *Kippered salmon platter. Ask for a scoop of whitefish salad to accompany your platter, and mix both on your bagel. This is the breakfast of champions Lunch and Dinner *Roast beef special on rye (russian dressing and cole slaw) If you're a fan of NYC Jewish deli's, you'll fall in love with Famous the second you walk inside. As you're eating your leftovers the next day, you can't help but fall in love with Famous all over again.

text: I was in St. Louis for a wedding recently, and stayed out in the Frontenac area. There's not a great deal there in terms of restaurants aside from chains, so I was pleased to find this place on Yelp for Saturday brunch. It's in a truly nondescript strip mall, and looks fairly standard for a diner-style restaurant, but was well worth the trip. In general the food was good and portions were generous but not to the point of being piggish (Cracker Barrel, I'm looking at you). The beef bacon was nice and crispy; eggs were done just as asked; hash browns could have been a bit more cooked; bagels were good but not exceptional (few are, really). They actually had bialys. The coffee was decent and not at all burned, a perennial problem at brunch places in my experience. The staff were very friendly and attentive, but not pushy. The entrance is a bit confusing, because there are two different signs, side-by-side, with different names. Both have the name "Pumpernickel" but one has the names of a pair of guys, the other doesn't. It looks like two different restaurants, but they are indeed the same. Overall, it's worth stopping in if you're anywhere in the area. The variety of diner- and deli-style offerings is impressive, and you could easily eat here once a month for a year and not really repeat much.

Decor is definitely leaning trendy but I found it stable and comfortable enough. They have marble in bathroom and kitchen areas which is nice. Hated that they charge for wifi though. We had curtains so light was not a challenge but street noise was a bit problematic at times, especially as it got to be the weekend. I sleep like the dead but others in my party found it a bit annoying. Staff was great, we made sure they knew we wanted daily maid service and got it no problem, the room was kept spotless. Tip nicely and you will get incredible service. The concierge was super sweet and helpful about various adventures we were looking into. text: On a recent Sunday morning we decided to go out in search of new life and new places to enjoy breakfast. With a little help from Yelp we stumbled upon HBN; this is our story.... At first blush, all you see is surly DelCo locals enjoying their "usual". Then, having but a split second to savor that moment the waitress calls out to you as she heads in from a smoke break, "yous want coffee????" Seeing no sign we assumed that you can sit anywhere you'd like, (we were correct). I had barely taken my coat off before the waitress came over with the coffee and asked what we wanted. I looked at her in bewilderment, "can we have a menu?" Her reply, "no menus, you can have whatever you want." I glanced over my shoulder looking for a list of options over the counter....... no list. I looked at her and, feeling the pressure, I said, "do you have french toast?" yes. "um, can I have a side of bacon?" yes. "and a fried egg?" yep. She took my boyfriend's order which was the same except for pancakes instead of french toast then turned around and yelled, "hey Ma! Can I get 2 eggs fried, 2 sides bacon, one french toast and 1 pancake!" A sweet, upbeat voice from the grill responded with, "you got it!" Suddenly, I found myself in love with the path my Sunday morning had taken. This was just delightful! I looked around and realized that people had ordered way more then my mundane breakfast under pressure. The food came and while this place isn't going to be up for any Michelin stars in the foreseeable future it's some damn fine basic breakfast. To top it off at the end of our meal the waitress came over, looked at us and said.... "uh, 20 bucks?" - I'm looking forward to going back time and time again!

text: Lara B is right on the waiting area seating - it is pretty shabby (no, not shabby chic). But I can't hold that against the place. I've never bought new tires here, but have went here several times when I was having issues with my tires. Ask for Mike Duncan - he is a great guy and will give you a straight answer, recommending what is best for your car AND affordable for you. He's told me when my tires were worth repairing or when they needed to be scrapped. A patch here won't set you back too far - I don't think I've ever spent more than $15 getting the necessary repairs made. Washington & Kitley isn't exactly a very nice location, but if you are having tire issues and need help, go to Firestone and ask for Mike. He'll take care of you.

So here I am, eating an overpriced sandwich I didn't order, in a nearly deserted cafeteria style "bistro" in the center of our depressing-ass downtown, and it occurs to me, is that Celine Dion on the radio? text: First of all, while our family had fun snorkeling, the "captain" that runs this tour is basically a smart a$$. I can't remember the captain's name, but the service was to Egmont Key ferry from Fort de Soto Park. We took it on July 9th, 2010. Our family of four have never been snorkeling before. While we didn't expect one-on-one training, it would have been nice to receive a little more encouragement instead of the captain's "just jump in, you'll be alright" mentality. I could visually see that he was irritated at well over half of his 37 passenger crew. See, out of the 37 passengers, probably 22-25 of them had never been snorkeling before. So the captain's wife (who was very nice) "trained" about half of them while the captain trained the other. Training consisted of: 1) Spit in your goggles to prevent fogging 2) Remove hair from goggles 3) Jump in. Seriously...that's it. Now, granted, there isn't much to snorkeling. And I can live with the brevity of the "training" because I understand time is limited. But here is what I didn't like. But before I start, keep in mind the girl on the phone for the reservation and the brochure led you to believe you were really getting a lot for your money. 1) The smart-a$$ remarks from the captain. Things like "just jump in people, you won't drown." 2) Can't you swim? 3) MANY visual indications of frustration with passengers. 4) Just generally being a jerk. 5) Asking for tips before the trip even started. BUT, I saved the best for last. Here are the comments directed towards my family personally. 1) To my wife referring putting a floaty on my SIX YEAR OLD SON: "We have two floats, the noodle and the strap on float. The strap on is much more enjoyable! HAHAHA" Yeah, the 13 year old in me can laugh at stuff like that but seriously, you said that to my wife while my son was there? I didn't hear him say that. She told me afterwards. 2) To me referring to my SIX year old son's poor swimming abilities: "You should just keep him in the kiddy pool". He said that with a straight, frustrated face. As if he were serious (which he was). The brochure didn't mention experience needed. And finally number 3. 3) Referring to my SIX year old son's lack of experience: "That boy is just going to drown." Yes he said that. EXACT quote. Totally serious face...NO indication of kidding. He walked away after that. At this point I SERIOUSLY was holding my self back from smacking the wrinkles off his face. But a few things held me back. One was the almost $200 dollars I spent for this thing up front. Second was ruining the trip for my family (by going to jail or being sued) and ruining the trip for the 30-something other passengers. So I bit my tongue and tried to have as much fun as possible. The comments to my son really sent me over the edge. I normally don't even post reviews like this for bad service. I usually just don't go back. But the service from this man was so bad I had to do SOMETHING. Now, I do have to say his wife was great. The only saving grace of the whole experience. She even swam out to us and asked if we needed anything. Oh, and I am assuming she was his wife...I'm not really sure but they "seemed" married with some of the comments they made back and forth to each other. How someone nice like her can tolerate a total jerk like him is beyond me. Anyway, my recommendation is to never use their service. There are TOO many companies in the Fort DeSoto, FL area that offer the same service to have to take that crap from Hubbard's. Stay far way.

text: Hey Chris here...former tarot card reader turned private business owner in New Orleans, Louisiana. I remember what this quaint store used to be like and maybe this is why I may be prejudiced in my review. Boy things have they changed. In the past there was more variety; it was less of a tourist gimick and more of a healing store where you could get some pretty good crystal wands and stones. Now I feel it has gotten even pricier and the staff at the register are more business like and less inclined to be interested in the art of true healing. I used to live in Ohio and could find my share of metaphysical oddities and good bookstores that just made you want to stay, gawk at the merchandise and really pore over a good occult book. This store is too commercial for my taste and the crystals are just your ordinary, run of the mill fare that makes for good gift giving but should not be taken seriously if you are a spiritual healer. The store left me feeling rather empty on this trip and the readers just appear to me to be a bit burnt out or jaded. I did opt for a reading with one of the older readers but it was such a cold read-- a generic read that it left me feeling unenlightened shall we say? The store is rather small and yes they do have quite the selection of teas but they have changed to plastic cups rather than china like they used to have so it just did not feel like the same indulgence or luxury from the past. I don't understand why they call this place Bottom of the tea cup since in the past it was the tradition in the 1930's to have your tea leaves read for you when you finished drinking your tea. Now it's tea in plastic cups without all the glamor and it really does not have the same vibe it had pre Katrina. I hate to write such a bad review but there is nothing out of the ordinary or special about being in the store in the Quarter.
label: NEG

text: I am going to go against the grain a bit here, but Five Guys is not that great. I think that the reason that Five Guys is so popular has more to do with lowered expectations than actual quality. Let me explain. I think over the past few decades we have been exposed to enough terrible hamburgers and fries from fast food establishments and lousy restaurants that our expectations of a good burger have been lowered so far that a passable hamburger seems amazing in comparison. That is exactly what Five Guys has, a passable burger. The fries are good and of course they are fresh, but aren't fries supposed to be fresh. I suppose this is why the "craft" burger has taken off all over the city and across the country. When people forget that a product is supposed to be good you can get away with charging a premium for anything that is above average. That get's me to my other point. After all is said and done, with fries and a drink, Five Guys is a $10 meal. There are dozens of places in Nashville that have excellent burgers for around $10. Hell I rarely walk out of Gabby's for more than $8 and that is a far superior product in every way. Most of the sports bar's and pubs in the area have Burgers for less than $10 so I don't really get it. Overall, I think that Five Guys is okay, but they are not particularly special or particulary a good value. Long live the era of low expectations.

text: A buffet place that doesn't quite match up... A private party on a Sunday afternoon, Wong's Genghis Khan Kitchen was an interesting experience. On my first pass through, I see the Mongolian barbecue station, then come across the soup, then the hot foods and moving on next to the cold stuff - nigiri sushi, desserts, kim chee, and self serve ice cream from Dreyers. When I grab my plate, I peruse through their dim sum selection: tiny siu mais (pork dumplings) that were dried out and needed to be left in the steamer, har gows (shrimp dumplings) that were bigger but acceptable, and char siu baos (bbq pork buns). They also had sesame balls, egg rolls, deep fried shrimp (too much batter), shrimp with the head on still, beef and broccoli, braised string beans (good stuff), fried rice, chow mein, chow fun, beef skewers, and a few other random things that would make up their Chinese selection. When you get to the soups, they had won ton soup and what I would call a Chinese chowder soup. The soup was good, but watch out for the cross contamination of bowls. When I reached for a nearby bowl, I noticed raw meat juice in the bottom, and realized they put the bowls from the nearby Mongolian barbecue station right here. So, be wary. For the barbecue station, you fill up your bowl with raw beef, raw pork, raw chicken, raw veggies of your choice, and some sauces of your liking. They throw it all onto this giant heated surface and stir it up for you and that's about it. That's Mongolian barbecue for you. I'm not a big fan of it myself, so I passed on it. Japanese nirigi - believe it or not, I passed it on. What looked like mediocre slices of fish on giant balls of rice just didn't seem that appetizing for me. So, I bypassed the whole thing. Huge assortment of cookies and random pastries were laid out nearby, along with fresh fruit including the canned stuff like lychees. You'll also pass the forementioned kim chee just about now. Then you get to everyone's favorite spot - the self serve ice cream station. There's a nice note on the window asking you to put a disposable plastic glove on your scooping hand so you don't continue the germ spread factor already existing in the water where the ice cream scooper is, but trust me, no one reads that sign. (I happen to read it and use the glove myself, but everyone else who had ice cream didn't even notice the sign or the gloves present!) They offer chocolate, strawberry, vanilla, green tea, mint chocolate chip, and macadamia nut. The ice cream is pretty hard and you need a strong arm if you're gonna get any. (Which makes me wonder how any of the kids ever got to it.) The green tea tasted weird, maybe it was old? Overall, I probably won't be going back. It's not a place I would recommend for buffet eating in Reno.
label: NEG

text: If you are looking for a fun winery to check out in the Indy area, Easley is a good choice. It's in a central location, on the east side of downtown, so that's a big plus -- most other local wineries are somewhere in the 'burbs. You can find several varieties of Easley wines like their Reggae Red, White & Blush at local grocery stores, but stop in the winery to experience a wider selection. There is also a nice shop inside filled with all of your essential wine accessories. The staff is really nice and will teach you all about their wines and winemaking process. I've never been on one of their winery tours, but I would like to - they are offered every Saturday from 9:00 - 6:00 and Sunday from 12:00 - 4:00. If you are from out of town and visiting Indianapolis, I would recommend making Easley one of your "tourist" stops while you're here -- it's an off the beaten path destination, but a quick cab ride from any downtown hotel. It's too late in the year now, but Easley has a Groovin in the Garden event every Tuesday and Saturday during the summer months. I am putting this on my list of must-do events next summer -- local bands play, wine is flowing, and the real kicker... several area restaurants will deliver food right to you. In 2008, Santorini, Bazbeaux and Circle City Pizza all participated and you could also get fresh breads and artisan cheeses from Fair Oaks Dairy. Sounds delicious -- I must go in 2009!

text: It's freezing here in Philly. So cold, that it was actually too cold to snow the other day--something I didn't even know was possible! Of course, being accustomed to the heat of Miami, I am desperately looking for ways to warm up. I've taken up residence in front of my fireplace at home, wearing obnoxious down-feather slippers, and layering on North Face's, but I think the best way to get warm is from the inside. And that means eating soup....lots of it!! Since neither my mom or I felt like shedding enough layers to cook a pot of homemade soup ourselves, we decided to go out for some Vietnamese Ph at Ph & Beyond in Willow Grove. If you aren't familiar with Vietnamese food, you might be wondering just exactly what Ph is. Here's a little food for thought: Ph is a beef noodle soup that is considered the "National dish of Vietnam." The rich and aromatic Ph broth is prepared by boiling beef and chicken broth for twelve-hours along with spices and herbs such as ginger cloves, star anise, cinnamon, lemon grass, and cilantro, which creates a distinctly unique flavor. The delicate broth is then traditionally served with rice noodles and either sliced brisket or eye round steak. Most places also provide an accompanying dish of bean sprouts, lime, basil, cilantro, and jalapeno peppers to be added to the soup by the customer, according to desired taste. As you may have guessed by the name, Ph & Beyond is particularly well known for their Ph, which is truly incredible!! When you walk into this restaurant and look around, almost every single person (90% of which are Vietnamese) has an oversized, steaming plastic bowl of this soup in front of them. And there are no doubts as to the authenticity of this place, because Vietnamese chatter is the soundtrack to your meal. If it's good enough for natives, then it's got to be the real deal! I order my Ph with well-done brisket, lending it the specific name Ph Chin as opposed to Ph Ti, which is with rare eye round. The brisket is sliced super thin and it compliments the flavor of the delicate broth just beautifully. One of the only problems Ph presents for American diners is the actual eating process--aka getting the contents of the bowl into one's mouth. The soup is served with two utensils; chopsticks and a porcelain soup spoon. This means that you need to coordinate eating the noodles with chopsticks in one hand and spooning the broth to your mouth with the other. It is a process that takes some getting used to and you can expect to feel entirely frustrated as the Vietnamese natives around you effortlessly devour their soup in a timely fashion. I am the fastest eater out of anyone I know, but the required eye-hand coordination of this feeding process brings me to a grinding halt and forces me to eat slowly. Being a spice lover, I enjoy my Ph with jalapenos, which adds an unexpected heat to the delicate broth of the dish. I also like adding the fresh bean sprouts, which nicely contrast the soft rice noodles in their crispness. Oh, and the lime juice is a must because it adds the perfect amount of acidity to the soup, without a noticeably strong lime flavor. Also, my adopted Korean sister showed me that the best way to eat the meat of the soup is to pick it up with your chopsticks and swirl it in some hoisin sauce and/or Sriracha (Asain hot sauce) on a separate plate. I love condiments and dipping sauces, so I chose to eat mine this way and loved it. Also good at Ph & Beyond are the Búns, which are rice vermicelli noodle dishes, occasionally served in lemon grass broth like soup. My dad ordered the Bún c Biet, which is a house specialty containing grilled pork, grilled chicken, petit egg rolls, grilled shrimp, rice vermicelli, shredded lettuce, cucumbers, pickled carrots, and mint. All of this is then topped with crushed roasted peanuts and served with homemade fish sauce. It sounds like everything but the kitchen sink, and it kind of is, but some how all of the meats, flavors, and textures work together in an incredibly delicious way. I enjoyed bites of my dad's dish just as much as I enjoyed my own soup. This dish is also a little bit easier to eat, especially if you ask for a fork! My mom decided to have a light lunch and ordered the gi cun, which are garden spring rolls containing shrimp, pork, vermicelli noodles, cilantro, cucumbers, mint, and lettuce wrapped in rice paper and served with homemade hoisin-peanut sauce. The portion was really large for an appetizer, especially at a price point of just $4.50!! I would definitely order these again. All of the portions are enormous (left-overs for sure) and the prices are really cheap. My Ph was only $7.50 and my dad's fully loaded Bún was only $9.95. These are recession prices people, so go eat here to warm up for cheap this winter!

text: Photolounge has been my lab of choice for many months now. I initially found it when the folks over at Ritz didn't have what I was looking for, they directed me up Chestnut a few blocks where maybe these guys had it and I've been going there for all my photo needs ever since. FIRST IMPRESSIONS: Very clean, never cluttured, and more focused on development and printing than the afforementioned Ritz, which seems to focus on camera sales, among broader service offering. Photolounge (formerly named CBOP) carries a great range of films, including my favorite-- medium format, along with frames, some camera bags, etc. THE SERVICE: Where Photolounge really shines is their service-- while quite not as rapid as your pharmacy's one-hour photo lab, they are still quite fast, but the focus on quality is unmistakable, and moreover, their service is very reliable, which has kept me coming back time and time again. The attitudes of the folks who work there is generally delightful, always friendly, always optimistic, always constructive, no exceptions. At other labs, I've gotten attitude, I've been the victim of employees taking out their frustrations from other customers-- that has never happened here, and I doubt it ever will. And, as I've brought so much repeat business to Photolounge, when things go wrong, as it becomes inevitable after enough time, they are always willing to rectify the situation, fixing the problem, whatever it is, at no extra charge. I first got hooked on Photolounge for their film selection, but I stayed hooked because of their excellent, friendly service. PRICING: Generally very reasonable, it certainly didn't break my bank, which is tight enough as it is. My mother wanted a couple of photos I took printed up for her birthday, and between the processing, printing and the frames I bought, the pricing was right where I thought it should be. I can't really remember how much it used to cost at Ritz, but the difference, be it higher or lower in price, is negligible. THE BOTTOM LINE: If you are in the Rittenhouse area, and you have film you want developed, re-developed, scanned to CD, blown up, printed, or anything in between, the choice is simple-- it's these guys. They know their stuff, they are passionate about their craft and the quality therein, and I highly recommend them.

I realize some may like this texture for their pizza so I'll move on to the other major problem, the sauce. It was sparse to say the least and had no zest whatsoever. I like to taste the sauce on my pizza! Finally, the cheese was bland as well. Clearly it was just one shredded cheese but it tasted like a skim or low fat type mozzerella. It just had no flavor at all. Even the salad was just ok. I don't think it was as bad as the pizza, but I was really hoping to like something that we ordered and it just didn't work for me. Sorry NPC, but you've got a lot of work to do.

text: Excellent, excellent customer service. But to explain their excellent service, let me first explain why this hotel is getting 4 stars instead of 5. My husband and I stayed here with his parents, and we each got 1 room at the same rate. It turned out that our room was about 25% smaller than their room, even though we were paying the same rate, and there was a funky, sulfurous smell overwhelming our room. I couldn't take it. We asked to switch rooms the next night, and it was no problem for the staff. I appreciate the promptness and courtesy of the staff, but I can't give 5 stars to a hotel that would charge the same rate for a hotel room that was tinier and literally stank. In our new room, the toilet had problems flushing properly, and the light bulb in the bathroom went out. These aren't huge problems, but the staff took care of it right away with a no-problem attitude. I really appreciated their attention to these details. Now, on to the good stuff: 1) Location. Right on State Street, close to the beach in one direction and all the best shops in the other. 2) Food and drinks. Complimentary breakfast includes waffle maker with great waffle batter, satisfying pastries, yogurt, fresh fruit, and an assortment of cereals. Drinks include hot coffee and tea in the morning and evening when it is cool outside, and iced passion fruit tea in the afternoon when it is warm. 3) Free wireless. I never understood why the high-end hotels always charge for wireless Internet, and the lower-end hotels give it for free. Nevertheless, Hotel Santa Barbara gives it to you for free, so thank you. Overall, it was a cute, comfy place, and I would stay there again - so long as I didn't get the tiny stinkroom!
label: POS

text: For the price, this hotel falls very short. There are nice things about it, but the service lacks. They didn't start out very well when I flew into the Nashville airport at 8:30 pm, visited their shuttle desk, paid $40 for a round trip shuttle, was told the shuttle would be there in 10 minutes, and an hour later, I finally had to call the hotel asking where they were. Their answer? One of the two "shuttles" had mechanical problems and they didn't know someone was waiting at the airport and they would be there in 7 minutes. 15 minutes later, a full-sized tour bus came to pick me up. They are definitely doing their part to contribute to global warming. By the way, I found out a taxi ride from the airport is $25. I wish I would have known that. When I finally got to the hotel, I waited another 20 minutes to check in. This might be normal during the late afternoon. But, it was now nearly 11pm and I was the first in line the whole time. There were about 5 or 6 people running around behind the front desk, but I have no clue what they were doing. What I DO know is that they weren't checking me in. Just a warning to anyone who has difficulty walking. There is a good chance you will have to walk a really, really long way to find your room (that's if you ever actually find it). I'm sure they make a pretty penny on the motorized wheel chairs they rent for $45 a day. I'm fortunate and able to walk, so I headed off with my map, dragging my luggage and got quite a workout, but eventually found my room. I suggest bringing a compass and a canteen for the trek to your room. I saw no sign of bell service. My room was clean and efficient. When I say efficient, I mean small. If you are looking for a spacious room, forget this hotel. The bed was OK. I'm not big on pillowtop mattresses, but I know they are the current trend. I tried to change the temperature in the room several times, following the very explicit directions. It never worked. If you aren't into 71.7 degrees, you may be in trouble. The bathroom was OK. Basic soap, shampoo, conditioner. No shower cap, no other amenities. The hair dryer didn't work, so I had to call for a new one. The food I ate in the restaurants was OK. The only really good food was served at a convention dinner I attended. The service in the restaurants was OK. Probably the best service I got all week was the room service. It was speedy and effiicient. If you want your room made up anytime before 5pm, this hotel will probably not be for you. Housekeeping has two speeds: slow and stop. Probably, the most pleasant surprise was the fitness center. There are plenty of up-to-date machines from treadmills and eliptical machines to weight machines and free weights. The fitness center overlooks the pool and is clean and well-lit. The daily mandatory resort fee includes use of the fitness center and pools. The pools looked very nice, too. Internet access was good and fast. The convention center was nice. Nothing stood out bad or good. The atriums, waterfalls and plants are all nice if you are into fake and sterile "nature". I guess it would be worth a stroll through the place if you were staying in another hotel. I was here on business, so it was OK because I was usually in meetings. I would never spend my own money on this place.
label: NEG

text: I should have known better. I have been to this place a handful of times over the last few years and it never changes. I went in last week for a late night dinner at around 8 o'clock (okay my "late" night dinners tend to get earlier as I age). I walked in with a few friends and the bar was packed but no one was sitting at the tables eating dinner. Ugh, I mumbled to myself as I know what kind of evening I would then have. The waitress came over about a minute after our arrival and asked us where we wanted to sit. Oh did I mention that she said this to us with a look of disgust and inconvenience? How could I forget that little detail. Hmmph. Anywhoo, we chose a corner booth near the window. All the tables were bare- no place settings, no candles, no condiments...I wondered if they had maybe started to close up for the evening? It couldn't be. This was an Irish bar...where men like to drink and get drunk fast..there was no way it was closing. The waitress came over with menus, place settings and asked if we wanted anything to drink. As I quickly perused the menu I saw that they were offering Three Olives Vodka drink specials on Sunday night. Oh my. It was Sunday night and I liked vodka..so maybe my night was going to make a turn for the better. And so I asked about what kind of drinks were part of this special. She responded that they haven't used Three Olives Vodka in three years and therefore there was no special on that this evening. Ah yes, and so it begins... Don't you think you should update your menus at least twice if not once a year? Don't you think that you should greet your customers with a welcoming smile? Don't you think that you should act as if YOU actually own the restaurant and want people to come back so that they can spend more of their hard earned money in your establishment?!!! The night only got worse. So bad that our original waitress came back about a half hour after we last saw her. She was making time with her beau at the bar. The bartender actually became our waitress and I ended up at the bar asking for the check an hour and a half later. Listen McCloskey's owner...maybe you should not try to be both a restaurant and a bar. Concentrate on the things you do well...and if you can't do that then try to hire some competent and friendly staff.
label: NEG

text: They were close here. We first went to Dooky Chase's. Closed. Then all the way over the Jacques-Imo's. Not quite what I had hoped -- that is, self-consciously cajun. text: I went to the Philly Diner today to find out how they could mess up a turkey club. Based on what they presented me, here's what they would suggest: 1. Use some sort of bunny bread "rye" and don't really toast it all the way, so that it smashes down flat. 2. Put a tasteless, spongy, soggy substance in your sandwich instead of using turkey. 3. Keep your bacon well humidified so that it's nice and moist. 4. Do not, under any circumstances, allow the sandwich to become contaminated with any mayonnaise. 5. Make sure your lettuce is well aged and your tomato is unripe. 6. Serve with a soggy mess supposed to represent cole slaw and a cucumber pickled with week-old dishwater. I would give them no stars, but since the last time I went there they've switched from those horrible fries with the crust on them to regular old frozen fries. Which are not that great, but definitely better. It's impressive how this place has been continuously going downhill and staying open. They used to be pretty lousy when they opened down the block, but they're even worse now, and the place is grungier and more run down. Which I wouldn't have a problem with if the food was edible. But on Penn campus, it's the same old story: Students will eat almost anything, especially if they're drunk and it's 3 AM. Or any time of the day, really. Also, the prices are outrageous. Service was fine, though. Just a horrible, horrible, wretched, sniveling place.
label: NEG

I just can't dig all the smoking especially since most of the people smoking were adolescent blond girls. Yeah, sort of weird, but that's no reason for a 2 star rating snice it's different laws here. I had the Peppercorn Burger done medium, but instead I got a hockey puck. They said by some regulation they can't go lower than medium. That would've been okay, but I got hockey puck. Hockey puck is way past medium, way past well done for that matter. Couple that with soggy fries and what you do you get? To be nice, not really satisfied. Sorry, but I guess I'm a food snob. text: mmmkay...Yes this hotel is in a great location, we were able to walk to the capitol building and lots of local eateries and shops. I asked how she was "doing today" and she rolled her eyes and responded "its a long story." She paid for her food delivery in the middle of our transaction, told us how NOT to use the elevator (the rules are very specific) and sent us up to our room. Our room. Well, it was probably in the 40s outside at that time and our room was maybe...low 50s? not a huge issue if we didn't have to open the window because the room SMELLED LIKE MOLD! blegh. our refrigerator didn't work (and started making really loud clicking noises in the middle of the night, and we had to unplug it) one of the bedside lamps was also broken (the switch had been pushed into the base), the sheets were stained, and the floor was sloped so when we were lying in the bed our feet were over our heads. . .and sitting on the toilette was. . .tilt-y... the water in the shower took almost 10 minutes to heat up, there was filth and trash and dust bunnies and other things in between the walls in the sink fixture in the bathroom. We stopped by the breakfast area the first morning, I'll be it near the end of the allotted "breakfast" time, and the employee there gave us a look that said "dear god not more people' soo we left and found a charming place down the street (Thanks Yelp!) and ate breakfast there every morning of our trip. We bumped into that first employee a few times more, and the results were pretty much the same, we got grumbled at... eyes were rolled. When we checked out, there was another employee behind the counter (she looked and acted like a manager) she was very sweet and helpful, she even offered to call us a cab to the airport. text: I wanted to have a set of gel nails done and I went wandering around the city looking for a place that was open on a Sunday. I happened upon this place and their menu said they did UV gel nails. It was my first time at this salon and my first time getting UV gel nails. I asked them if they applied gel and let it heat cure with UV and they said yes that is how it worked. I sat down and May (I believe) started to work. She started to lay down acrylic on my nails and I had to stop her and ask what she was doing. She didn't understand my questions and had to ask the shop manager to come assist. It turns out that they don't do a true UV gel nail here. They lay down acrylic (supposedly special UV acrylic) and then a layer of gel on top to make it shiny. You do get the heat curing on the one layer of gel. I wasn't happy about this but figured I was already invested in it and decided to just go forward. I'd have acrylics in the past so they weren't foreign to me and I knew they were strong and decently long-lasting. The work was done fairly efficiently and looked decent from afar from when you look closer you see air bubbles, crooked nails, too much acrylic at the edges and in some spots fairly thick. OK, I can deal with all that shoddiness since it serves me right for trying to do this cheaper. BUT, it's now 3 days later and half the nails are lifting and I'm very unhappy about this. I will now have to go back to this salon to get them fixed or go somewhere else to have them removed and re-applied. Editing to add: I did go back to the salon today and spoke with David the manager. He wouldn't provide me with a full refund without taking off the nails. He offered to correct the nails and make them right. I agreed and he did a lot of cleanup work on them - things that I found out should have been done originally. He removed the gel topcoat leaving me with just arcylic on my nails. He refunded me $15 for the upgrade to gel and polished my nails when he was done. He did a good job and I'm happier with how the nails look now but will not likely return. They should have been done right the first time and they weren't.
label: NEG

text: What can I say that hasn't already been written in one of the previous 145 reviews? As a guy who tends to avoid the super flashy restaurants in favor of less conspicuous foodie haunts, I had never been here before (or really felt any desire to try it out). I always thought "yea yea, Stephen Starr, Maseratti's out front, blah blah blah." And yet, when the time came to celebrate a special occasion, I knew I couldn't get away with just another quirky hole in the wall (No offense to all the holes in the wall that I love! Don't hate me, I had to do it.) So the big occasion is that I got engaged this morning. I know, what the hell am I doing yelping today? I proposed this morning, then it was off to Parc Brasserie for brunch to start the celebrating. Maybe I had the rose colored glasses on today, but everything was fantastic! The poached eggs with polenta and roasted peppers and greens were delicious. The polenta was very cheesy and garlicky, and they blended perfectly with the poached eggs. My fiance (first time referring to her as my fiance!) had an omelet with smoked salmon that was light and fluffy. For desert we tried the nougat with vanilla, figs and pistachios, which was wonderful. Creamy and smooth, with refreshing bits of fig made this a nice treat to cap off our meal. Overall, it was a wonderful experience and a special way to celebrate. Although a little pricey for brunch, it's not that bad if compared to a nice meal at night. A special thank you to our server, who did a wonderful job pampering us, and got so excited about being the first person to know of our engagement that she had to hug us both!

text: At 7pm on a Tuesday, it was notably crowded. My party of 2 was definitely smushed into a table but the restaurant crowd thinned out by the start of the Eagles game at 8pm. Our waitress was nice but obviously frazzled and a little overextended for the first hour of dinner. Regarding the food.. First and foremost: their veggie burger is as great as other yelpers have claimed. I ordered the Brouwer and vegan patty. I loved the topping options, the patty held together well, and it definitely has my vote for best veggie burger i've had in philadelphia. Amazingly good. Nice work, Belgian Cafe. I love sweet potatoes and hummus so I was very anxious to try the sweet potato hummus; sadly, i wasn't impressed, although my date absolutely loved it. I thought it lacked flavor, but the array of vegetables and pita that came with it was nice. He also really enjoyed the chicken fingers. They looked great and definitely home made and fresh. & what is all the hubbub with the fries? I thought the dipping sauces were good and a nice change from plain ketchup, but the fries were standard fries. All the fries in our basket were shorter than an inch, and eating french fries with a fork ruins the experience for me, so that may just be an odd personal preference. Anyways, the fries were fine.. but it was just a basket of fries so don't get your hopes up. Other little things: the naked ladies on the wall were odd, but I applaud the support of local artists and the explanation int he menu. The beer selection was wonderful. I'd be more likely to hang out in the bar if they had more than one tv. Overall, it was a really good experience. I'll definitely be back again for the beer and veggie burgers!

Something about the texture seemed off. However, that sauce on the za was delish. Trust me, I'll try another za next time. Def bar style; not traditional. Another person had a wrap. She said it was devine. She ate it all. So, it must have been pretty good. Or, she needed to pad the two seriously tall and stiff martinins she had. Lol. The food is decent for bar food. Then, once your done, you can walk out back and chill outside at a picnic table. This is a fun area and can accomodate lots of folks. The staff works hard here. This place can get busy...not too packed. They do have servers that do their best while being positive. What can you ask more? Dig it. You'll see me round.

text: So I'm all dolled up in my Easter best, because of course it is Easter, and we head for our reservation at Herbie's for brunch. Upon arriving, I was immediately overwhelmed by the number of pastel-clad Easter folks scurring around the buffet. I felt like I was in Driving Ms.Daisy, and some member of the clan was about to come out of the corner and serve me up some grits. The buffet was a disaster by the time we got there. Our reservation was for 1:30, and being the descent sort of church-going folk that we are (descent I mean, in that we go once a year... actually I hadn't been back since the last Easter...I guess that makes us descent and hypocrites at the same time) Anyway-- our reservation was late because we went to church to celebrate the resurrection, darn it. I didn't expect to get punished later by a brutally torn apart compilation of a 'once was' breakfast smorgasboard. By the time I got a warmed plate into my hands, the filet of salmon was barely recognizable as such, the salad was gone, the dressing was a smeared mess all over the table, hot pans of egg dishes were over steamed and miserable, and my dear, poor, stomach particularly unhappy. I did manage to down some cocktails, though. Two grapefruit and vodkas and a glass of pinot grigio. Our waiter was attentive but seemed stressed, which made my boyfriend stressed out too because he is a waiter and knows what it's like to be over-worked. I felt like the whole thing was just a little out of hand. Perhaps they needed more staff, perhaps they should've made more food. Either way-- it was a pretty under-par experience. I have been to Herbie's when it was really good-- and I'll probably go back again. I certainly won't get suckered into one of their holiday buffets, though.

text: When I live in NYC, I used to think the MTA LIRR (Long Island Railroad) was bad. After moving to Phila, SEPTA was worse. It's robbery, there are stations that don't have ticket vending machines and/or ticket office is closed. I hope someone sues SEPTA here. The buses are worst, they run one bus every hour on weekends or on a weekday when a bus gets canceled (you call SEPTA and they haven't got a clue). SEPTA can't even manage to try to connect railroads to buses or buses to railroads. The regional railroads are usually littered with tickets (purchased on-board) and daily papers (e.g.: Metro). This system does not run 24 hours! Grrr. I have to admit, I have come across some nice bus drivers and conductors of SEPTA. There are a couple of SEPTA Regional Railroad that are good in making up time when they are delayed. A few bus drivers came across as complete arseholes. It's the damn agency and the way how things are being ran. Fire all of the board members and reorganize. SEPTA did one thing right, I commented about schedules being unfriendly printer format and suggested PDF versions of schedule. It took them long enough. You can file a complaint online about its service and they usually respond a few days later. However, the service has not improved. If it's a railroad complaint on the Northeast Corridor tracks, they usually blame Amtrak for delays. SEPTA raised its fare on July 9, 2007 and it still has crappy service. Tip: If you are traveling from NYC (NY Penn Station to Philadelphia), it's cheaper to go via NJ Transit and SEPTA as supposed to Amtrak. You might save a little time with Amtrak and maybe a more comfortable ride, but you can do at about 1/2 the cost with NJT and SEPTA. text: This is definitely one of the best Southern Cantonese style restaurants in the city and the best on the Southside both for Dim Sum and dinner. Edmonton's Chinese food scene is limited. China is a big country and home to a billion people. There are varied and diverse cuisines from China. Edmonton does Cantonese and Hong Kong style really well and this is one of the jewels in the crown. Easily as good if not better than anything in New York, San Francisco or Vancouver. What we miss out on is really good Schezwan, Hunan and Shanghai. The restaruant was recently renovated and has a spacious well appointed dining room and newer clean washrooms. The food is fresh, hot and well seasoned and executed. Southern Cantonese is more about subtle flavours with good use of garlic, ginger, onion, tomato, oyster sauce and black bean. A lot of the food is braised, steamed or wok fired. A wok needs to be white hot to cook food properly, leaving the incredients firm, crisp and flavourful. They do this very very well. Dim Sum is fresh with a good variety. They have a Dim Sum chef and the food is made for service, not frozen and thawed. Prices are really quite reasonable and a bargain for the quality. Service is prompt and attentive. Chinese do not have a service culture akin to French service, but wait staff are reasonably available and really helpful with the menu. The best food, like all Chinese restaurants, are off the English menu. Ask for suggestions or for what's good off the Chinese menu, or look around at what the Chinese tables are eating and ask for those dishes and there are a lot of Chinese patrons. There is only a couple of comparable restaurants downtown and on the Westside. The Golden Rice Bowl is definitely worth a visit. Come with a large group, sit around a big round table with a lazy susan and order a variety of the excellent dishes.

text: one of the best seafood restaurants i've been to- a truly uplifting experience where the intricate combination of fresh seafood and colorful pallets will make you drool on your entire napkin. One of the best examples of showcasing distinctive flavors of oysters from different areas in the US. Also had a bite of the first course lobster, where its lightly cooked on the outside, leaving the inside a semi-raw-like texture- amazing combination with sea urchin and oranges. For the entrees, the Skate Wing and Monk Fish rocked my belly. The pan-fried Skate WIng had a rich flavor, partnering with a parmesan broth and truffles on top. The Monk Fish in contrast has a lighter flavor- but this is carefully balanced with the flavorful lamb belly, octopus and artichoke. Finished with the Chocolate Torte and Blueberry Cobble- a simple yet regal ending. the result of the distinctive food combinations will put a smile on your face- and you won't know why until you walk out and begin to drool again. and again. to sum up: -warm, insightful service -cozy atmosphere -wide range and carefully selective seafood -creative touches on every flavor combination -pricey, but worth every penny

text: I remember going to the Silver Legacy on opening night. It was back in 1995 and believe it or not they even had rooms available. It was jam packed and unbelievably easy to get credit. The first time I was able to open a line of credit without having my credit checked. Those were the good old days. Well here we are 11 years later and I still go to Silver Legacy whenever I can. When you arrive at the Silver Legacy, you are given a choice to self-park or valet. I recommend valet especially on the weekends. If you self-park, you will spend your time going up each floor looking for parking with 50 or more other patrons only to find yourself on the roof and having to turn around and drive back down. Why? Because there are no spaces available. Believe me, I have been there; done that. Once inside you will find yourself on the midway filled with shops, restaurants, and of course the slot machines. One thing I really like about the Silver Legacy over the others is that they have a wide variety of games from The Munsters all the way to the new Party Time / Jackpot Party. If you like table games, they have the usual Blackjack, Poker, Roulette, and of course Craps. In fact, the Craps games downtown offer the 3-4-5 odds, which in theory gives you a better chance in walking away from the table a winner. But the key word of course is CHANCE. For more information, ask your friendly dealer. After all the excitement of gambling, you probably will be hungry. My recommendation would the Sterling's Steakhouse. The atmosphere is elegant and the food is delicious. Adjacent to Sterling's is the Oyster Bar where you will find some of the best Bloody Mary Oyster Shooters. The price is right and the seafood is excellent. Finally, if you are staying at the Silver Legacy, you will be treated to some of the nicest rooms in Reno. The Silver Legacy is the tallest building in Reno and if you are lucky to get a room on a higher floor, you will have some of the nicest views of the mountains and city. An added bonus is the security. Silver Legacy is the only hotel that has security at the elevator. You must show your hotel key before you can get to the elevators. Keeps out the riff-raff. Speaking of security, this place does not mess around. One night I was awaken by the sound of another hotel guest banging on my door to get in. He had one too many, if you know what I mean. Well, instead of getting out of bed and beating this guy senseless, I called security and within 30 seconds, 2 guards had him in custody. No kidding 30 seconds. Now that is security. In closing, I like to go to the Legacy every chance I can. But the only reason I don't is....well....read my review about The Atlantis in Reno. Good luck and good times!

text: Citizen's Bank Park to me is enemy territory. Myself, being a die-hard Mets fan have to be pretty ballsy to come to your arch-rival's stadium in the thick of a pennant race. Since I want to visit all MLB Ballparks, the trip has to be done. First off, driving to the ballpark was classic, my friend was wearing his Mets jersey and this kid in the car next to us, flips him off. As soon as that happened I knew it was going to be a fun night. We arrive at the ballpark which is on the very South of Philadelphia located in their sport complex. Finding parking wasn't bad, we just followed a Mets fan so we can feel "safer" - yeah that parking lot is hostile, but some of the insults that those fans threw our way were just classically lame, it was comical! This being a huge game, we unfortunately didn't get a seat in the ballpark, but we did get $15 standing room only tickets. Not bad, at least we could roam around the concourse and see the game. We hung out at Section 109, and we had an excellent view of the game. Phillies fans would say things our way, but at that time Mets were winning by a decent margin. There are a lot of rude fans there, but I met my share of really cool people who just love baseball all together. Phillies Girls would walk up to us wearing their Chase Utley 26 shirts and say: "We hate the Mets, but we love David Wright" -- typical. Frat Kids would walk around, try to insult you, and end up doing the opposite - it was a fun environment if you are thick skinned. If you aren't, or you are with kids - please be careful, the language can be salty. The ballpark is beautiful despite being the home to a rival. Open concourses, plentiful food options, Ashburn Alley is a unique part of the stadium, you have food options and a team shop out there. To me, it was fairly similar to Chase Field, but with a cozier and less-mall like atmosphere. This felt like a baseball stadium and not an airplane hanger/mall food court built around a baseball diamond. I can't wait to see more games here deeper into the season, plus I can't wait until my Mets get their new stadium in 2009. Citizen's Bank Park is a gem of a ballpark despite the Phillies. As Of August 08: Citizen's Bank Park ranks #2 out of 5 ballparks I've been to.

text: So it's either really early in the morning (like 5 am early) or the middle of the afternoon and you're hankering for some brekkie. Or you better be, because after doing some extensive research I discovered the best time to drop in is around 2 in the afternoon, otherwise you're in for a looooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooong wait. Longer than it took to read that word. It's not a bad wait, though. They provide some sidewalk chalk that you can just go nuts with on their outside patio and waiting area. Some scribbles I read (and totally didn't write) were "Bay of Pigs was SWEET!", "Better red than not fed", "The COLD War", and a weird dude with a mustache. The wait wasn't too long, and I basically kicked my friend's sorry butt in tic-tac-toe a few times, so we were called in shortly and seated at a cozy table. The menu at Sam's Morning Glory is short but impressive. Lots of frittatas, sandwiches, pancakes, waffles, and other delicious looking dishes. There's also lunch dishes that are probably good, I wouldn't really know though. Some notable favorites include pecan waffles complete with peach flavored butter; monkey French toast with caramelized mangoes and 'nanners, and salmon and goat cheese frittata. We got none of them though! I adored the Gardenkeeper's frittata with greens, ham, and potatoes and my anonymous friend ordered a focaccia breakfast sandwich with eggs, cheese, and bacon. I recommend them both, especially if it's part of the breakfast platter, which includes a choice of grits or potatoes, a biscuit, and some stewed apples. All were very tasty, though the biscuit was definitely the standout piece and deserves a standing ovation. These aren't you're regular biscuits, not the kind you learned to make in seventh grade foods class or some KFC coupon deal, oh no, these things are monsters. The texture is more like a heavy cake, it's quite dense, but the flavor is 100% biscuit. Slather some butter on that sucker and you've got a small baked product fit for God, or, for you atheists, Bill Maher. Sam's Morning Glory also offers five or so desserts that include 'nanner cream and pumpkin cream cheese pies. They also have lots of homemade goods. The ketchup (which is basically marinara sauce), flavored butters, steaming hot chocolate (don't guzzle the fog machine in that son ova gun) are all home made. The environment is small and very mom and pop, not too far from south Philly and South Street, and the service is nice. This joint has reasonable prices for quality food (check plus!) and one unforgettable and all around magnificent breakfast experience. Our meal came to about ten bucks each, and extremely filling. If I could describe Sam's Morning Glory in two simple words: So moist. Or brilliant biscuits. Or delectable diner.

text: I made a discovery that makes So Italian's pizza acceptable ... almost. After not finishing the pizza (in part because I over-ordered, in part because it wasn't worth stuffing my face with crap), I took a couple slices home in a box. My figuring was that I could give it to that homeless guy I always see at the interstate exit ramp. though I eventually decided against this because even hungry people have standards and deserve to be treated with dignity. So, after a long drive home, sitting in the near-freezing trunk, the pizza made its way to my refrigerator. Fast forward two days: It's cold, I'm hungry, and I've been snowed in by a blizzard. In an act of desperation, I open my fridge and see those two slices of pizza -- looking as bad as ever. I sprinkled them with a little water, put them on a sheet of tin foil, and broiled them in a toaster oven for about five minutes. The difference was extraordinary! Somehow, my home remedy corrected for the pizza's shortcomings -- a few days in the fridge dried out the once-soggy crust, and a few sprinkles of water and reheating melted the cheese to an acceptable level. Does it make So Italian worth returning to? No. But if you make the same mistake I did and go there anyway, know that all isn't lost. Freezing and reheating makes their pizza every bit as good as the frozen pizza you get at the grocery store.

I highly recommend the duck pastrami and the pancetta mac and cheese. These indulgent dishes are good enough to comfort anyone's soul. If you're looking for more of a savory sandwich, definitely try the pastrami which I frequently order. Don't forget to save room for dessert because they have great cupcakes and popsicles to end the meal. Cochon Butcher is more of a smaller venue good for 2-4 people. It is a restaurant you come to self indulge in and give into your food inhibitions.

text: I'm surprised by the Yelpers who think this place is overpriced. A dinner for two, stuffing ourselves on sushi, usually comes out to about $40. For good sushi in the Midwest I don't think that's unreasonable. The rolls here are mostly delicious. My friend and I don't go for tuna, which makes us unusual in the sushi world, but there is such a variety of rolls here it doesn't matter. The Wasabi Special, Washington Avenue, Alaska Roll, and the new Yummy Roll are all favorites. Hurricane is tasty but has a bit of a fishy taste from the crawfish. If you like crawfish you should be fine but if you're not a fan, beware! you can definitely taste it. Service is fast, the rolls are the right size (not the supersized ridiculous rolls some places serve, but big enough to please), and the quality is consistently good. Service is fine - they keep our glasses full, but don't hover. Atmosphere is nice in a town rife with dives, chains, and noisy family restaurants. The best recommendation I can give is that I dine here at least twice a month, or else I start craving it!

Even the veggie burger was a solid 3.5 stars, but after trying both, I boxed up the veggie again and concentrated on thoroughly enjoying the moist meaty goodness. I will never order a burger anywhere else. Period. 5 stars! Duck fat fries with cheddar and short ribs was also very tasty. But after finishing the burger, these did not hold up well with time and given how rich the food is, I had to look away from these. 3.5 stars Pickled cherry tomatoes - flavor bombs! These were eye-opening and when you have a bite of the burger, then one of these, WOW!! 5 stars So while I'll never battle the crowd to get in, I won't go anywhere else for the perfect burger.

text: I've been to parks all over Nashville, and it's possible that none of them are individually as good Charlie Daniels Park in Mt. Juliet. Sure, if taken together, the Nashville Parks offer a whole lot more, but they're spread across a county. Charlie Daniels has all the neat features of Centennial Park without the problems. It feels like a community feature rather than a destination point for tourists, it has a football field for the high school. It has an indoor community center with an indoor basketball arena. But those are there for organized activity. For the family, there's an excellent "Planet Playground" for both under three and larger children. They have several tennis courts, and wisely turned a couple of them into a small skate park. They have an outdoor basketball court, a sand volleyball court, several covered pavilions with picnic tables and grills, and an outdoor stage "amphitheater." Every now and then, you find something new, like the pirate ship or the jogging track. There's a lot to like about the park, and if your family is there and you need to kill an hour, it's a nice place to go.

text: I was extremely disappointed with our treatment by the staff this morning. This is the objective facts of what happened: My party of 3 arrived at 11:20am, and we were told by the hostess that there was a 20 minute wait, which I thought seemed a small timeframe, but I believed her. After 10 minutes of waiting, I noticed that we were #5 on the list of 3+ parties. There was a concurrent list for parties of 2. They seated a party of 5 who arrived after us prior to seating us. We witnessed another party of 3 who arrived before us and had been told 15 minutes speak to the hostess about the fact that they had been waiting over an hour, and she responded in a frustrated tone, "We can't control how quickly people eat and move along." 80 minutes after we arrived, we were finally seated. I asked our very nice waitress if I could speak with the manager on duty. She wanted to know why, and I told her about our waiting experience. I told her she could pass the message along herself or she could send the manager to our table. A slight man, who apparently had told someone who arrived about an hour after us that there was "no wait for you", came to our table and apologized for his hostess's lack of hospitality and because she hadn't offered us coffee the whole time we waited. He also responded to jrg's comment about how the hostess almost got punched after she copped the attitude with the other party of three, "That would have been cool." He also told us that it was her first day on the job. Perhaps it was a confluence of bad behavior, or perhaps it was a new restaurant still growing their busy legs, but I will definitely think twice before I return on a Sunday morning. I'll ask myself, is it early enough to go? is it late enough to go? how hungry am i? how much patience for way underestimated wait-times do I have this morning? Additionally, I noticed a large bottle of vodka and a bottle of champagne in the drink area despite the lack of alcoholic options on the menu. I found it to be odd but forgot about it until right before we left when I heard the cork pop and 4 glasses of mimosa be served to a table in front of us. Perhaps this might be a place where it helps to know somebody? I'm disappointed because I do want to like this place soooo much...

text: I was introduced to Tommy Gunn's by way of the now defunct South Street location. The place had this amazing yellow/orange light inside, homemade cola, three kinds of sauces (Texas, 'Bama, Carolina) and they played the hardest '50s Blues-Rock records I've ever heard in my life. Sadly, they closed. Years later, I'm hiking through Rittenhouse Town, down towards the falls, and upon completing my detox, BOOM - Tommy Gunn's, right on Ridge Avenue. Let me tell you, there is no better way to finish a hike than to eat some (as Bill Cosby aptly says) "B-B-Q." Tommy Gunn's is ideal for takeout for sporting events, backyard barbeques, and casual parties. They're not cheap per se, but they're worth every penny. People love the fries, I do not. I swear by TG's cole slaw all the way. They also have deep fried macaroni and cheese, which will wipe off more years of your life than smoking a carton of Pall Mall's, but definitely worth trying. I miss this place from Center City, especially when so many of the alternatives lack the ambiance that made Tommy Gunn's my favorite Friday lunch spot.

text: My husband and I had an overall pretty great stay at Le Richelieu. We booked through some big booking website, so I knew not to expect a really great room. The first room we had was ground floor, small, smelly, next to the pool, across from a maids station, with a view of the parking lot. I kind of suspect that this was the worst room in the hotel. That said, it was clean and perfectly adequate but I was also pretty disappointed. We spoke to the woman at the front desk who checked us in and she said she could try to move us the next day, but there were no guarantees since they were fully booked. We had a wedding to go to the next day, so we told them we pretty much needed to know that morning if we would be moving or not. Well, we got up the next day and got dressed up for the wedding, then checked out of the crappy room and left our luggage at the front. Keep in mind, just about any room would have been better than the one we were in, but when we returned to check out our new room it was beyond our expectations. We were moved to the honeymoon suite! I think we got lucky, and it was vacant during our stay, but the staff also seemed very happy to be able to move us there. We were thrilled. The other rooms in the hotel that I peeked into (non ground floor) seemed just as nice as the honeymoon suite, just smaller. Nice comfy beds, high ceilings, most have balcony access, and WALK-IN CLOSETS! Also, all rooms have an iron and ironing board. The bathrooms could use updating, but there is nothing actually wrong with them. I would say that this hotel is a great deal for the price, location is excellent (lower quarter), staff are outstanding, and rooms are great for a stay in New Orleans. Not too old and beat up to be icky, but not so new that you feel like you could be in an anonymous hotel anywhere in the world. Highly recommended and I would definitely stay there again.

text: Doylestown is an old and wealthy town, with old stone buildings, two stories high. The narrow streets have parking meters, which are not easy to come by. Poor Richard's Talk of the Town, is the name of this shop. It is a two door open store, where you can walk into one side and browse the displays, walk through an open doorway, mid store and into a copy cat version of the last set up, only the "stuff" has changed. This store seriously reminds me of many of the same shops you will find in Doylestown and on Cape Cod and should be labeled "junk for sale" or "inside Flea Market". You may find a hidden treasure or two in here, but I highly doubt it. While visiting, I was the only potential customer, in the store. He decided his time was best spent arguing with his significant other on the phone, about why he should not bring home anymore flower pots. As for me, I've been there and I left empty handed, as for Poor Richard, I do not foresee a name change anytime soon and I am sure he is the Talk of the Town.

text: Stayed here last week during a trip we took to go boarding in Tahoe. This was a bit further than staying closer to the ski resorts in Tahoe, but it was way cheaper and rooms were more available. We got in pretty late, as we got stuck in a snow storm driving to Reno. I made reservations in advance though so I wasn't too worried. Check-in went smoothly and we even got upgraded to a suite for no extra charge. Now, why the 2 stars you ask? As soon as we stepped into the room, the first thing I noticed was that it reeked of smoke. I requested a non-smoking room. The smell was so bad, I obtained an instant headache and eyes started to hurt. When I went down to the front desk, the staff member insisted there where absolutely no more rooms available and there was nothing she could do. So, she sent up a maid to spray the room, which she claimed would get rid of the smell. Instead, the spray left a really strong fragrance that mixed horribly with the smoke and left me feeling nauseous. At that point, I went down and and said I was checking out and staying somewhere else. That time, a different man helped me and he said he'd figure something out. Thank goodness! So we ended up getting a non-smoking room that miraculously became available... yeah right. Since the room and bed was smaller, we needed a rollaway. So, we called in to request one and it took almost an hour to come. When I called to see what happened, they said there were only 2 housekeeping staff members working in the entire hotel. In the end, we went to bed at almost 3am and woke up late to go boarding the next day. Now, despite the room and rollaway issue, the rooms actually were pretty decent. They were spacious, clean, and would have been a good alternative to staying at an expensive room in Tahoe. But with the luck we had, I think I would have rather forked out the extra money to stay in Tahoe.
