text: El Greco is a neighborhood shop, and it's just a few blocks from my workshop. I stop by every once in a while, and it's an experience. Today, as usual, there were a bunch of people inside. Three behind the small (but tall) counter, a driver or two outside, and three or four customers in the long, narrow area inside. I order two slices, which are put in a box. (A bit of a downer for me - what, they don't want me eating in front of the shop? Put it on a plate, please...) I go outside and stand by my bike and eat them - warm, gooey, and very sweet. The cheese is thick and chewy, the crust is soft and light, and the sauce is sugary and squirmy. The slices are floppy - they fold, and don't crease - and drip red-orange oil as I squeeze the fluffy crust to keep the whole package together. The first bite requires me to hold the crust side above the rest of the slice, so that it doesn't unfold and go limp. Eating the slices produces a texture that resembles, almost, mollusks. As I stand there eating, I observe the scene. A tall, gaunt man sits on the stoop, then stands and mills around the storefront, smoking a cigarette. Three customers who came out of the shop just as I was entering sit on a stoop next door eating their slices and talking. The traffic on 2nd St. whizzes by, passing the small community at Jefferson - the slice shop, an auto tag store and a barbershop. I like El Greco in a way. It's not exactly gourmet, but talking about the quality of the food misses the point of the business. It isn't quality - some might go so far to argue that it's hardly pizza. Either way, it's food, it's part of a neighborhood. And sometimes that's all you need.

text: Diagonally across grid-locked Route 70 from Han-Ah-Reum (or H-Mart), set back in the Barclay Shopping Center, is the Chinese answer to the Korean mega-mart. I think the Koreans have won. Not that there's nothing to like at the Asian Mart, mind you. For one, it's big. Which means plenty of varieties of instant noodles, canned pickled vegetables, fermented sauces and snacks. They have a five star snack section. Pocky! dried Mango! Salty Prunes! Dried Squid! For the same prices as you would see at Philly's C-town, the deli offers up decent roast pork, duck, soy sauce chicken, curried octopus and porcine offal. The small buy-by-the-pound hot foods section offers mapo doufu and braised pork butt. Just remember to get there early since most of the deli and hot foods are gone by mid-afternoon. Coincidentally, these are items that for obvious reasons, cannot be found at the Han-Ah_reum. Chinese 3, Koreans 0 But what could be a vibrant Asian market experience, turns flat when you visit the fresh veggies and fruit section, and their meat and fish markets. Sure you can get the usual Chinese veggies like Shanghai bai cai and Chinese broccoli and bitter melon, but they like to wrap everything in plastic bags (so that you can't pick certain things and they control the portion you buy). That really irks me. The H-Mart, on the other hand, has that laissez faire thing where I can choose which ever green bean I please and only get 3 ounces if I that's all I need. And, the veggies look fresh, unencumbered by the plastic bags. Chinese 3, Koreans 1. Both places have small fish sections where you can pick a living fish which they will give last rites to and clean it as well. I do find that the H-Mart have somewhat fresher iced fish than the Asian MArt. You can tell by the clarity in the fish's eyes. That is, if you can get yourself to look it in the eye. CHinese 3, Koreans 2. In the meat sections, they both have butchers on hand as well as prepackaged meats. But it's hard to find basic meats, like chicken legs and pork chops at the Asian Mart and often the meats behind the case don't look appetizing. The only time I bought any meat there was when spare ribs were on sale. If I need ground pork for dumplings (jiao zi) or mandoo, I brave crossing Rt. 70 to get to H-Mart. The Koreans have tied it up. But the main reason why I wind up saying "Annyong ha shimnikka" to the missionaries in the parking lot and head into H-Mart is the crispy, demurely sweet store-made rice treats. The stoic rice-cake man pops them out like nobody's business and the free samples keep my whiny kids sedate. Pop! There goes another rice cake. Pure theater! Koreans 4, Chinese 3. So, Asian market, you need loosen up a little. Free the vegetables from their clear plastic straight jackets! Get rid of the rigor mortised, bleary eyed fish on ice! Play on your strengths! Have a Pocky themed event! Cooking classes with durian! Show us that you can partay and we'll come.

text: I have been coming here since early fall, and after a few months all I can say is that I really miss my studio back where I used to live. I have been to some pretty good classes here; for the most part, though, they range from mediocre to bad. Strangely, the most (consistently) terrible class I have been to here is taught by Bill Raup, the studio owner. In a 90-minute class, he forced us through all the major poses, from Sun Salutation A all the way to Half Pigeon, in the first 60 minutes. He spoke so quietly I could barely hear him, demonstrated nothing, and rushed us through -- no one was able to keep up, I looked. The final half-hour was spent on random poses that made no sense after what came before. I actually left early because instead of feeling calmed and energized, I was feeling tense and angry. Yoga is not about speeding through 75 poses and doing none of them mindfully. That is a recipe for injury. The other teachers here provide a better experience than this, but it is still not what I signed up for. They do little to correct people's poses, don't vary the flow at all, and do little to challenge intermediate yoga practitioners. They also don't suggest modifications when it is clear that you are struggling with a pose -- for instance, I can never do camel because it crunches my lower back every single time, yet not one teacher has ever said, "and if this pose hurts your lower back, try X." There is also absolutely no vibe to this studio. If you are looking for the sort of place where chummy regulars chat each other up before and after the class, this is not for you -- the anteroom is deserted before and after practice. The blah decor of the studio doesn't help this. Finally, despite being billed as Baptiste "hot" yoga, the temperature never really rises above 85 degrees F. What!? I rarely even break a sweat, which is sad, because that's what I'm paying for. In conclusion: poor pacing, sloppy teaching, low temperature, somewhat depressing vibe. And -- only 2 classes per day, both in the evening (huh?). I bet they could attract many more people in this student-heavy area if they offered classes throughout the day.

text: If you're familiar with Grimey's New and Preloved Music, you probably know about Mike Grimes' downstairs and aptly named music venue The Basement. The Basement, though small, holds some really impressive and very intimate shows on a weekly basis. Though The Basement is one of the less spacious venues in Nashville, it makes for some of the most memorable and neat shows you'll see. It's non-smoking indoors, but there is a pretty fantastic little patio for smoking and relaxing outside. The sound is always nearly flawless, and it's small enough that you can hear the band no matter where you venture. The Basement serves beer only, but they offer Yazoo as well as the usual domestics. (Correction: they serve liquor. Hurrah!) The bartenders and sound guys are always friendly, and if your band is booked to play The Basement, you'll get $1 domestics and superior monitor mixes. The Basement books local and national acts and also has comedy shows pretty regularly. While you'll typically see Tennessean acts (small and large), if you buy tickets in time you'll also be able to see the more intimate shows of bands like Guided By Voices and comedians like Fred Armisen and Zach Galifianakis. Though there is a foosball table, it's eaten the money of patrons more than once. Other than that, there's little about The Basement I don't absolutely love. If you get the chance, come by one of Grimey's record sales/shows which are co-hosted by Grimey's and The Basement. They are always a blast.

text: Boyfriend picked this restaurant for our last dinner while I was visiting Tucson. Before dinner, we were given a little bowl of olives, as well as some fresh bread with sun dried tomato butter -- both were tasty! We decided to order a few things to share instead of individual meals (that's just how we do): Bruschetta (Crescenza Cheese, Asparagus, Prosciutto di Parma) -- i normally hate asparagus, but this was so light and tasty! plus, i'm a sucker for anything with prosciutto on it.....which leads us to.l.... Pizza (Figs, Prosciutto and Goat Cheese) -- i wasn't nuts about figs, but boyfriend really wanted it so i totally caved (hey, he made the pouty face, i can't say no to that!). Being from Jersey, I expected Arizona pizza to be a total farce of what I consider real pizza -- but i was wrong! crispy thin crust, perfect amount of toppings (though i did pick off some of the figs, too sweet for me), and i discovered that i actually like goat cheese after a terrible past experience! Calamari Salad (Crisp Calamari, Baby Arugula, Grilled Lemons) -- OH. MY. GOD. barely any breading on the calamari, nice and crispy on a bed of fresh arugula with a really nice dressing (lemony vinagrette? i dunno). so so good. It was the perfect amount of food for us, and didn't leave us feeling overstuffed and gross. We decided some dessert was in order: Vanilla Gelato (boyfriend's pick) -- creamy and packed with vanilla bean specks, just the way it should be. blueberries too! yummy :) Tiramisu (my choice) -- okay, now Tiramisu can go wrong if you don't make it right. text: In the past year, Banh Mi had become the latest food fad that everyone seems to enjoy and being in Philly, we benefit from a respectable size of Vietnamese population residing in South Philly. That being said, the best Banh Mi in Philly is in a small store in Chinatown called Q.T. Well, it's not scientific observation of course. All I did is comparing a few bakeries in Chinatown, Ba Le, O Sandwiches and Ziet Cafe in South Philly as well as Sampan around 13th and Walnut, so I'm open to suggestions on places that I should try. But as of now, I'm sticking with Q.T. Two friendly ladies behind the counter made up the Q.T. sandwich team. They make each sandwich to the order to guarantee maximum bread crispiness and freshness. The prices here are slightly more expensive than conventional Chinatown standards and since it's made to order, there is a 5-10 minutes waiting time but it's quite worth it. Like other reviewers have mentioned, each Banh Mi has slightly sweet and sour pickled carrots and cucumbers, fresh cilantro for spice and jalapeno pepper for heat. The non-vegetarian ones are smeared with pate. I usually get the special Banh Mi which contains a combination of three different meats. The bread is toasted and crunchy which compliments the crispy vegetables, the creamy pate and the meat. The storefront can be slightly improved and it'd be great if they can speed up some in the sandwich making department but other than that Q.T. is definitely a welcomed addition to the Philadelphia Banh Mi scene.

text: [This review covers both Pat's and Geno's, so it's posted at both pages.] So for some reason, my crazy friend, Elliott, and his friend, Bill, decided to drive from Richmond, VA to my house (oh, probably about 5 hours) Saturday morning to go into Philadelphia for cheesesteaks. Why? To put the ages-old debate between Pat's King of Steaks and Geno's Steaks to rest once and for all... Not that the debate will ever really die... We ended up hitting Pat's first, then trekking all over the city, only to return to Geno's before heading home. Gotta work off the calories, yanno! In the end we all came to pretty much the same conclusion. Overall Pat's really is the King of Steaks. Geno's decor was overwhelming and gaudy. We did not find the giant picture of a cheesesteak surrounded by flashing neon lights on the roof to be particularly endearing and certainly did not add to the flavor of the sandwiches. The bright neon orange slathered all over every possible paintable surface did not help, either. I greatly preferred and appreciated the understated and unassuming simplicity of the decor (or lack thereof) that we found at Pat's. They still had what looked like the original Pepsi sign with their name. We were also taunted by a 10 year old walking by with a Geno's cup while we were minding our own business, sitting on the curb eating our steaks. None of us appreciated the blatant politics of Geno's either. For those unaware of the controversy, a few years ago Geno's was sued for having a sign on their window that said "This is America, Speak English when ordering!!"... While I acknowledge their right to have whatever signs broadcasting whatever politics to which they ascribe, I find the hypocrisy of their Italian heritage coupled with their obvious prejudices to be quite distasteful. On to the actual food. The rolls from both place were exactly the same. More bread than meat - first bite: all bread. The onions at Pat's were actually fried, with that caramelized color and flavor I like in my onions (when on a cheesesteak, that is). Geno's onions seemed to have been lightly fried, more from incidental contact. They were still so crunchy that they were almost fresh. Not that I mind fresh onions, but fried onions aren't supposed to have that fresh-onion zing. They're supposed to be fried. The cheese. I could barely taste the cheese at Geno's. I opted for provolone, while my companions opted for the orange cheese-snot product called Cheez-Whiz. Pat's was generous with their provolone and the steak was hot enough to actually melt it before I was able to sink my teeth into it. Initially my companions did complain about the Whiz oozing out of the sandwich and onto the paper, but after eating at Geno's they realized that having enough Whiz to *taste*, much less have ooze out of the sandwich was a blessing, not a curse. Finally, the steak. This is the one point that we did have to give to Geno's. Pat's steak was shredded, more or less, which is really the way every cheesesteak I've had is. I have no complaints at all about shredded steak, however Geno's steak was sliced, so it actually maintained the classic "steak" texture, more reminiscent of roast beef than typical cheesesteak. This is really more about the style of cheesesteak than the quality. Though Geno's sliced style was a bit tastier, it wasn't what I think of when I think of a true Philly Cheesesteak. All in all I prefer the cheesesteak experience I found at Pat's King of Steaks. The fries were delicious (though I didn't try the fries at Geno's, I suspect they're about the same), the line moved faster, the onions weren't overwhelming, but just added to the sandwich, the cheese was tastier and meltier, and the whole experienced oozed real, authentic Philadelphia culture. If you want a taste of what Philadelphia really is all about, I'd recommend Pat's King of Steaks.
label: POS

I stepped into the shack and placed my order for pho with chicken and a canned Thai iced tea. My order came out promptly. Maybe too promptly. I could not wait to get home and dig in. Moments later I sat down on my couch, opened my plastic take-out container and fished around with hope. An imaginary trombone played "Wah, wah" as my dream drowned. Steam? Check. Noodles? Check. Lime? Check. Flavor? Chicken? Spice? Not so much. Obviously this place is not called "Pho Shack", but minus the harpist and curtains I didn't think my expectations were that unrealistic. Pho ain't that hard to make. Then again, maybe it is.

Soup comes - gummy and flavorless. Even the bf dosent like it - he eats everything - although he actually has a great palate! I thought restaurants wanted to know when the food was poor This restaurant said they cared but were obviously offended. "no one has ever said that before"...well.. sorry to say ladies but the soup blows!. They let us try the "old school tomato." Conversation between boyfriend and i: Him: try this Me: NO! it smells like Campbell's Him. It's not Campbell's.... its Chef Boyardee! text: Nico's doesn't sell Mexican Food. They sell hot, carby, flavorful happiness - wrapped in yellow paper. Nico's is up there near the top of the list of things we miss the most since moving away. I believe there are 3 benchmarks by which you can judge a Mexican food stand or taqueria: =-=-=-=-= Salsa =-=-=-=-= Nico's salsa is the dark red or green liquid kind; more of a hot sauce really. Don't let its lack of real consistency get you down, though. The flavor is great, but where Nico's red sauce reigns supreme is in heat. Theirs is hands down the spiciest of the Tucson Triumvirate (Nico's/Viva/Los Betos). I once saw some marines dining in after the bars, challenging each other to chugging shots of this potent elixir. One soldier slammed like 13 little containers and he never tasted again. That's called winning the battle and losing the war. In moderation, this stuff is killer. =-=-=-=-= Horchata =-=-=-=-= I think you see Horchata prepped / served one of three ways: out of the splashy Aguas Frescas dispenser thingy, punch bowl and ladle style, or *gasp* from some kind of concentrate out of a regular soda fountain (yuck). Nico's horchata is the first kind, which in my opinion is the best. The flavor is spot on with a nice blend of cinnamon and spice while never tasting chalky. Make sure you shake it up real good with the ice so it is extra cold, as this is how it tastes best. =-=-=-=-= Breakfast Burrito =-=-=-=-= Plenty of places will make you a burrito for breakfast. Heck, some may even throw some chorizo or eggs in it as well. Let me tell you what friend: Nico's is THE gold standard of breakfast burritos in our household. Never before have bacon, potatoes, eggs, cheese, tortillas, and salsa come together in a more perfect union. The size is usually about that of a small mortar shell, which is appropriate considering your mouth is about to get exploded with flavor. Sometimes you'll get shortchanged and get a skinny burrito - once in a while - but the vast majority of the time these things are plenty big. Some other places you ask for bacon and you really get ham cooked to a crisp - not the same. This is honest to goodness thick cut bacon. But the eggs - the eggs are one of the greatest differentiators: somehow Nico's has figured out how to keep the eggs fluffy and dry. This creates a welcome environment for incoming hot sauce, instantly melding into the consistency breakfast burritos are meant to be. This is as opposed to a pre saturated boggy marshland of runny eggs and cheese that might as well tell hot sauce to kiss off. These burritos also ELIMINATE HANGOVERS. Eat one post bars - even eat a half - and the Nico's elves start to go to work in your belly. The potatoes go to work first, soaking up any remaining alcohol in the mix. Cheese and bacon jump in, using their tasty grease power to line your stomach, further slowing the absorption of now unfriendly alcohol. The eggs and bacon release their protein, helping your brain repair itself, and the capsaicin from the hot hot sauce triggers endorphin production to help ease the oncoming headache. Go here. Health code blah blah whatever. These guys aren't surgeons, they make burritos. And guess what: they're the best at what they do.

text: We went to Murrieta's 10/16/2010. I have been wanting to go there ever sine I saw them with Sam Shad cooking those seafood enchilada's. So I finally persuaded my husband to go Chips and salsa at the beginning on the meal: the standard Pico de Gallo and then a smokey creation. The Pico de Gallo was my favorite however the smokey creation tasted more like something that would accent a taco rather then a chip. We ordered the pork half ribs and the seafood enchiladas with the cheese and salsa sauce as a n appetizer. Cheese and salsa dipping sauce: Not what I was expecting. The cheese tastes of a cheaper quality then Velveeta? Slightly sour, slightly plastic... if they change their cheese product-- great! Chips: A good standard chip however they need to make sure they don't mix the stale with the new-- we can taste the difference... The pork half rack: A thick well sauced slab of pork ribs served on crispy onions with a corn on the cob as well as black beans. The Pork Half rack: It is not slow cooked, it tasted as though it was steamed or baked with fluid to cook it quickly, then slathered with a chipotle BBQ sauce. I would recommend them to at least bake their ribs and then paint on the sauce in the last 10 minutes so it cooks and caramelizes-- this tasted as if it was spooned on after coming out of a hot water pan.... The corn? ugh-- old, very old. There were brown mushy kernels mixed in with the yellow-- and the corn cob was drying out-- when preparing to offer fresh corn, please ensure and keep your corn in a warm bath so it wont dry out... and check its age before you serve! The crispy onion strings: they came served under the huge slab of pork and when found, no longer were crispy but a mushy greasy memory of what could have been.. please serve those on the side so they can be experienced in their full glory... and a little salt would help too.... The black beans: black beans should be cooked with a few cloves of garlic and a lot of white onion and salted to perfection to truly bring out their flavor... these were just beans and water.... The seafood enchilada: After seeing the chef make them for Sam Shad , I thought they were going to be a spectacular cousin of what the chef used to make in Andeoti's of Harrah's. Wow, no way. barely any crab or lobster, the seafood is not fresh-- freshness is king for a good flavor to last the entire meal-- fresh garlic sautéed with the seafood in olive oil then mixed with the other ingredients would slap some life into this creation. The way he prepared it on TV was divine- his chefs need to be retrained and not skimp on the ingredients. Beans and rice were of course totally bland-- making a authentic Mex rice from a good chicken stock and the normal medley of ingredients will do wonders for your plates... and dont serve refried can beans--- make a good pot of pinto beans and they last for 5 days...... But then again folks I have worked and tasted the best food out there and also been served the absolute most authentic home cooked Mexican food and Mom will always do better then food commercialized.... I will not be coming back, because I have had and worked with better food then this....

text: Make a reservation, and make it NOW! This is the restaurant for students at the Art Institute Culinary Program. Sadly, few people know about it. For just $30, you'll get a six-course meal that is simply fabulous. The room is small (and, when we went, only half full). You'll get a large window into the kitchen to see the students in action. They pull out all the stops when it comes to food and service. Highlights were the trois potages (three tastes of soup, served cleverly in an espresso cup, a cordial glass, and a shot glass), each served with a delicious accompaniment. The chicken soup had a delicious parmesan crisp, the curried lentil soup a tiny samosa, and the New England clam chowder a bitty clam fritter. The lentil soup was a favorite. The 'creative contorni' wins points for best use of asparagus; the asparagus fettucine was wonderful. I also loved the rich ice creams for dessert, peanut butter swirl and chocolate silk. In between were many other great dishes from Dr. Pepper baby back ribs to sweetbreads. The students make as many dishes as possible for the experience. We didn't realize that we'd be served every item on the menu. No decisions necessary! Fear not. The servings are small enough to let you enjoy each course, but there's enough to leave you stuffed by the end of the evening. If you aren't an adventuresome eater, this is not for you. You don't get to order. But trust the chefs and try everything. You'll be glad you did. And check out the online menu in advance. This place is BYOB, so you'll need to choose your own wine pairings. Now stop reading and make your reservations!

text: Oh, Sage Diner - you tease. I thought I would go to a nice local New Jersey diner for lunch instead of one of the chain restaurants nearby... but though you are, in fact, a diner, you are not, in fact, "nice." I can't honestly say that anything was particularly awful about my visit to the Sage Diner, it was just really sort of... meh. I ordered a "deluxe" burger with swiss cheese and Russian dressing, and my boyfriend ordered a cajun chicken sandwich. The "deluxe" burgers are supposed to come with french fries and onion rings, but mine arrived sans onion rings. It also arrived sans Russian dressing, but my server brought me a cup of it on the side at my request... I let the onion ring thing go. The cajun chicken sandwich was what you'd expect - not bad at all, nothing eye-poppingly good. The french fries were just regular old pre-frozen steak fries and they were a little under-cooked. I think the most disappointing thing about this place was the fact that the breakfast menu was really limited at lunch time. Yes, it was noon, but I hadn't eaten breakfast and I was actually looking forward to something toward that end of the culinary spectrum... sadly, they seem to switch out the menus after "normal" breakfast hours, and the breakfast options get pared down to about half of the back page of the menu. Not cool, Sage Diner... not cool. The waitress was okay, if perhaps a little on the surly side. The decor needs some big-time upgrading, but that's honestly not unique to this diner in particular (it seems to be a common problem among them). I wasn't hungry when I left, and I didn't get sick from the food - those are pretty much the best things I can say about this place.

text: Going to MadMex for late night food on a Friday made me feel like I was back in college! My girlfriends from school were visiting (we regularly craved frozen big azz margaritas when we lived in Pittsburgh) and I am so very glad we ventured into University City. We had a party of 6 and were seated a little before 10pm with no wait. Our server was very accomodating and let us wait until 10 to order drinks at the special rate of $7 for a 22oz. frozen margarita. The strawberry is my favorite, lime is also tasty, I avoid the raspberry because it's got tons of seeds & mango because it has an artificial taste that can be on the bitter side (maybe you can tell I've drank a *few* in my time). It was just as frozen & tasty as I remembered, although not very strong. We were starving, so we ordered our food right away - if we wanted to hold out until 11 everything would have been 50% off. One order of the pickadippa to start fed our entire table. Then we each got burritos - overstuffed just like I remember. I'm a vegetarian and the idea of tofu in a burrito (especially when it's not seasoned very well) is pretty unappealing. Plus I don't think tofu & cheese mesh well. I opted for the angry hippie burrito - the spicy spinach is one of my favorites and the portabello mushrooms hit the spot. The place is dark & loud, it was a little hard to carry a conversation amongst 6, but it was still a fun time. We split the bill & ended up paying $20 (tax + tip included). It was well worth it for a couple of hours & a trip down memory lane. *They card @ the door after 3pm on Fri/ Sat and after 4pm all other days.

text: I've been eating here for twenty years, since Chef Giuseppe Rosselli hung his "Good Food" sign over the door. Those were great times for Olde City, and this restaurant literally sparked one of the greatest cultural explosions in the city. Locanda was the first restaurant on this strip of 3rd St. when it first opened. After one review in the newspaper, people caught wind of the place, and there's been a line out the door ever since. I've literally grown up with this place. My mom and dad would take my sisters and I in our teens, and I try to go as much as possible to this day. Chef Giuseppe is no longer with us, but his legacy lives on in the attention to detail in both the food and the service here. His wife and sons still run Locanda, and it's as if Giuseppe is still with us. The mushroom crepes are always great to start off with, the Fruiti di Mare never lets down, the Ricotta Gnocchis are killer, and even though these are my usual orders, the specials never let me down. Whether they have lamb chops in red wine sauce, a big juicy steak with a blueberry reduction, Chilean Sea Bass perfectly cooked and accessorized, or perfectly prepared Rabbit, the specials are beyond ordinary and beyond satisfying. The head waiter, Joe, is the most loveable guy you'll meet. Yeah, sure, he's loud and can sometimes seem pushy, but it's only because he feels as if all of the customers are his family. I don't know him very well, but I can tell that he feels this way. I've eaten here on plenty of dates, as well as plenty of large parties. I've personally booked a couple large parties, and have come away feeling as if I had received preferential treatment each time. I can say nothing bad about Locanda, and only wish I could visit more often. I've read a few reviews stating that the place is expensive, but trust me, it's not. And if you book a larger party, the prices are seriously some of the lowest you'd find in any restaurant in all of Philly. So, if you like to feel as if you're at a family gathering, and you don't want to break the bank, you will not be let down by the people and the food here.

text: The Masonic Temple is a gloriously kitschy attraction that rivals the Mütter and Eastern State in weirdness, and it's hiding in plain sight, right across the street from City Hall. Built in the 1860s as the grand lodge for the state of Pennsylvania's many masonic lodges, the Temple is filled with a repetitive series of meeting rooms that each pay homage to the stonemason's craft: there's a Morrocan Room, a Renaissance Room, a Corinthian Room, an Ionic Room, and a positively psychedelic Egyptian Room. Some of these rooms have stone and tile details, and the main hallway is mainly marble,though many of the theme rooms feature painted plaster. The Masonic Temple is an architectural candyland, offering a bizarro tour of how elite 19th-century Americans viewed other cultures, and a peek into the mysterious, kinda-creepy, kinda-laughable world of the Masons. You do have to take a tour (I think full admission is $8), as they won't let you wander. My guide was a funny and likeable mason who seemed more interested in chatting up one of the women on the tour than telling us about the building. But he was refreshingly frank when asked about the Masons and their history, and he had some good one-liners. I'm not sure I'd join his club, but it was fun to visit.

The paniir itself was good, the lamb was good, the vegetables and shrimps were good....but this Orange was all a bit suspect. I will say the leftovers warmed up nicely for breakfast and as usual it improved over night. Indian/Pakistani/Bangladeshi/Sri Lankan is so subjective as its prep varies so much so please go try them, it takes balls to open a Curry House in MJ and I wish them well but for now we'll have to be content with the memory of the Anurag in Cockfosters as Nashville's Curry Houses are still getting away with it . PS. I asked for a sweet Lassi and guess what got a Mango Lassi (no more orange), when the real Lassi came it was the best ever. PPS $14.95 for the lamb jalfrezi a little pricey!
label: NEG

text: I hear some people say this was a decent Thai place, and the food was good, and I just don't understand. I grew up down the street from this resturaunt, and because of the proximity to MacDill AFB I grew up with a lot of Thai friends. So over the years I've eaten a lot of home cooked Thai food (at 3-4 different households), eaten at plenty of Thai resturaunts (including this one at different times over the years), and this has consistently been the worst representation of Thai food that I've come across. Even a coworker who grew up in Thailand refused to go there on a lunch break because he insisted the food was subpar. If you find yourself in the area and are looking for good Thai food then you should try the place just across the street that used to be called Sunee's, they recently changed names and the new one escapes me now, but the menu remains unchanged (and great).

text: All you care to eat buffet. This place was awful! Plate after uneaten plate, I kept trying to find something from the massive selection that wasn't garbage. The usual allure of all-you-can-eat and the ability to try many different items is lost here. The "salmon" was white-fleshed and dry like a block of wood, the mac and cheese was cooked to mush and totally flavorless, the "prime" rib was also overcooked and dry, unlike the undercooked sausage I wouldn't touch. The soda machine was pumping out straight syrup almost, the milk was from a powder, I wouldn't try the high fructose corn syrup "juice" from concentrate. That's just the tip of the iceberg. A few tong-pokes at the catfish told me I was better off not wasting my time, the marinated mushrooms would have been better had they been tasteless, the turkey was really dry and salty, on and on and on... Basically, I found only a few items that I was willing to eat, but they never even came close to excusing the $13 cost of admission. The number of plates I went through was almost comical, had I not been so disappointed. The Courtyard Buffet is a great deal for really fat, disgusting people, who are happy shoveling the maximum possible volume of very low quality food into their pie-holes. Otherwise, $13 will get you a vastly superior, satisfying meal elsewhere nearby.

text: Oh this poor little bowling alley. I feel like it is so forgotten. This largely has to do with the location I imagine. This place is buried (and I mean BURIED) behind the Shop n Save and Ashley Furniture Outlet on Watson Rd. and sandwiched in by the train tracks that run behind there. People use this road as a cut through, not as a true place to go out. I feel like the bowling alley suffers because of this unfortunate location. However, this place is still somewhat bustling amazingly enough. It's not quite as packed as other bowling alleys I have been too, but in many ways, that is very good. That is very very good if you are hoping to get a lane without reserving one. Also, the place is very old and kind of dingy, but it's not as smoky as many bowling alleys in the area. That is largely due to their lack of population I imagine. On Thursday nights you can get a bucket of 6 beers for only $12, which is awesome. They have a huge assortment of balls to choose from, and you can even get bumpers if you call ahead and reserve them. (OK, it's embarassing that I know that, oh well.) Shrewsbury Lanes is the scrappy little bowling alley that keeps on kicking. It's very Big Labowski, if you catch my drift. No glory, but wow, the ones that know about it are quite loyal to their bowling alley.

text: alright. so I've only been to NY once in my life but I live with two native New Jersey-ans, New Jersey-ites, New Jersey-sonains? Whatever. The menu had a great selection. lots of different breakfast and lunch options, all of which seemed likely to appear on a menu at a diner in jersey. I chose to go with a mix: The corned beef hash breakfast with eggs. hearty. hearty. hearty. in addition to that you received your choice of side: i chose to be a true fake Jew and go with the potato pancakes. I was eating with a couple of them (real Jews) that is, and decided I needed to go all out. in addition to this ENORMOUS meal, you also got your choice of bagel or toast. seeing as I was being a good fake Jew, i obviously got the bagel. ALL for 8.99! The food came extremely quickly and we began to chow down. I enjoyed my first ever corned beef hash. My roommates had to explain to me that it wasn't necessarily supposed to be hot. It was good, and I really enjoyed my potato pancakes too. Although it would have been better if they had been served with some applesauce and sour cream! Come on Noshville! I'm trying to be a Jew here! I also sampled my roommates french toast. It was soft and yummy, and I enjoyed that the syrup was served in a coke bottle. SUPER COOL. The use of the egg bread really gave the french toast a great texture and I would definitely order it again upon returning. Everything was reasonably priced. Overall it was a good experience! text: The cobbler on 40th and Sansom is a great place. I was in dire need of a cobbler. After a couple months of Philly's wear and tear, my nice pair of oxfords' and beautiful Italian boots' insoles were fairly worn down and their heels were quite uneven in the back. I decided to try a place in my neighborhood, and brought my oxfords and boots to Cliff's. I wanted the heels and insoles to be replaced on both pairs and wanted taps added to them to preserve their heels better in the future. Since, I wasn't in a rush to get them back, the cobbler had them done for me in a week. It cost $48 / pair (including taps) and my oxfords were beautifully shined. They workmanship was good and I was pleased with their services. Although on my boots, he had started to paint the sole (the thickness part), but he realized that I wouldn't want that because it would cover up the soles' beautiful dark wood layers. I didn't mind... because honestly few people ever look that closely at your boots' soles. In addition to being great at repairing shoes, Cliff's almost felt like an old barbershop (or what I think a barbershop would feel like). When I went to pick them up, I had to wait a bit because the oxfords hadn't been shined. I sat in the shoe shine chair, and everyone who came into the place seemed to know the cobbler or the other people in the shop. It just had a really good friendly vibe. To speak more on the quality of their work, Cliff's definitely has a pretty devoted clientle that consistently comes back to his shop for their shoe repairs even if they don't live in West Philly anymore. I highly recommend them for shoe repairs and shines. They do a fantastic, beautiful job.

text: I will start by saying that my experience at Chappy's was almost 2 years ago. I have not been back since... even with a free $100 gift certificate from Chappy. We went here looking for a good cajun meal. What we got was shocking on several levels. I have never been treated so poorly by a restaurant manager in my life. I don't send food back and I don't often complain at a restaurant about the food I'm served. Like many of you, I've done my time working in kitchens and at restaurants in high school/college. So my family went to celebrate two family birthdays for me and also my Grandmother. I think it was a Monday or Tuesday night and the place was pretty empty. We ordered a few different appetizers. They were average. I want to say I ordered the Veal Bayou Caddy for my meal. It got to the table and for starters looked absolutely terrible. I tasted it and it just wasn't good at all. There was some watery, eggplant mush in the middle. The waiter came by and asked how we were doing and right behind him was the night manager. I told them that my dish was not what I expected and that it seemed like it was cooked wrong. The manager immediately left the table and came back with a small side dish of the eggplant/shrimp concoction and sat it down in front of me and said something to the effect of, "see there's nothing wrong with it... it's always like this." He then told me that I was wrong and that people love this dish. He left the table and everyone including the waiter kind of sat there stunned for a minute. Usually when someone complains I envision first an apology and then an attempt to correct the problem. I never in a million years thought I would get an argument and a display prop by a rude manager. The waiter then tried to pick up the pieces by asking if I wanted something else to eat from the menu. I told him no, I had lost my appetite. I was done at that point. The waiter was very apologetic and told us that they had had some issues with the guy in the past. Apparently Chappy was not there that evening, nor anyone of any real authority. The waiter brought the bill later and said that he tried to take my meal off the bill, but that the manager REFUSED to remove it. Yes... refused to take it off the bill. It isn't like I ate half of it and decided against it. it was almost immediately after getting it that there was an issue. Then the circus that ensued. We all left in disgust. My mom decided to call in the next day in hopes of talking to Chappy. She got him on the phone and retold the story. I'm told he was VERY apologetic and wanted to do anything to make it right. He even mailed my mom a gift card for $100 that I have still not used. I may suck it up and give them another chance. If that experience is good, I will write another fair review. Until then, they get a 1 star because they won't let me vote with negative numbers.

text: You can't give 2 and a haf stars on Yelp? Because that's what I want to give it. Like everybody else in America, I've been hearing about Philly cheesesteaks my whole life. So when I go to Philly this summer, of course we need to have one. We arbitrarily pick Genos instead of Pat's because why the hell not. Did you know that up in Boston we have this same kind of sandwich, only we call it a 'steak and cheese?' And we use real cheese...which is not a dig. I liked it with the 'whiz.' It was good, But it was nothing special. The meat came from a big pile of already grilled shaved steak, as did the mushrooms we ordered. It all tasted a little lukewarm. The roll was there. But at the same time, it's still a big, greasy sandwich and I was starving, so it was satisfying. Mediocre, but satisfying. And they did have some nice pickled hot peppers to add in, which made the sandwich lots better. Meh to Geno's. If and when I go back to Philly I feel sorta compelled to try Pat's to see if as rivals they are in fact superior...but I bet not.

text: Amazing find while in Philly. We originally made plans to have dinner at another restaurant in the area (Chloe), but discovered that they only accepted cash. Definitely a no-go when on business trips. We searched places in the area and found Fork 0.3 miles away...so we made our way here. Nice, smaller, space with a boutique feel to it. We were greeted by 2 large curtains that need to be shifted to the side to enter once past the door. We were immediately greeted by someone who gave us the option of any seat in the place - even the unique space in the "bay" of the front window. We decided not to since the seat sat 4 and it was only 2 of us. She proceeded to seat us near the back against the wall. The place was very nicely decorated; nice neutral colors and quality accents throughout. We immediately ordered a nice cab (not many cheap wine options here) and gave ourselves 5 minutes to order. We decided on the following: - Bread (free): 4 options (multigrain, wheat, white, rye)...served with a very sweet butter (brown sugar?) - Cauliflower Soup: We both tried the cauliflower soup...and both decided that it was definitely lacking something. Spice. Seasoning. Something...great presentation and nice touch with the chunky lobster pieces. I would pass. - Branzino: Unique Mediterranean fish that I had never heard of, served with head, tail, eyes, everything...tasted great. It was tough (and very annoying) to pick through all the bones though. Served with spinach and a heavy cream sauce. - Risotto: Great and simple dish. Great flavor. - Brussell Sprouts: Great; pan-seared with bacon and heavy oil. Browned to perfection. We were very satisfied with the meal and would highly recommend this place to anyone. I love the small feel of the restaurant; you could tell that the entrees were well thought-out. Will have this on my short list next time I'm in Philly.

text: I am a big rooter for all things East Nashvillean, as many people living in East Nashville tend to be. But I'm not delusional. Far East is just another restaurant with watered down Asian food that continues to litter the Nashville food landscape. To be totally immodest, I have eaten A LOT of Vietnamese food in my life. And, if I want Vietnamese food, I will have to continue heading to West Nashville instead of driving down the street to Far East. Now, the food isn't bad; it's just unremarkable. The food and the menu grasps for the Vietnamese flavor and taste, but doesn't quite get a hold of it. I'm not sure if it's because it doesn't know how to, or that it's catering to its diners. Regardless, as the rating goes, "meh, I've experienced better." The pho is not that great: it's too sweet, and it's expensive especially for the size of the bowl. It's a Vietnamese restaurant and not a strictly pho restaurant, so I don't penalize it for not having different types of pho. But, really, only one kind of pho?! The rest of the entrees I've tried have slight semblance to Vietnamese, but runs closer to something pan-Asian. For example, the flavor of the grilled pork (served with vermicelli noodles) was overpowering and totally missed the subtle flavors of the lemongrass and the smoked sweetness in the meat. However, I'm super glad that it's doing well and it has plenty of avid eaters there. It's always good to have a hip, hot and happening place in the hood. I just wish I could be one of them.

text: We went to Patou because my wife had heard that it was "fun". I'd never heard of the place, but I was willing to give it a shot. My first impression was that the entire place is a bit rough around the edges. Rough edges can add charm to some restaurants, but Patou's rough edges border on sloppiness. For example, the bathroom had rusty fixtures and wasn't very clean, even though we arrived at 5:30. It was the day before Valentine's, so we could only order from the prix-fixe menu. That was fine with me, as the menu sounded well thought out and interesting. However, reality proved different. We ordered the wild mushroom soup and billibi soup for our first course. My billibi was oily but tasted quite nice. The only thing that bothered me is that it was listed as a mussel soup, but no pieces of mussel meat were present. My wife's creamy wild mushroom soup, however, was a disaster. The mushrooms tasted like they had been almost charred and then over-concentrated. There was a distinct lack of cream and seasoning. I have a hard time believing that any of the chefs sampled it before sending it out, as overall the soup tasted like pureed burnt cardboard. Second course was a little better. My salmon tartare was also bland, but the wasabi chips that came with it were over salted almost to inedibility. Putting the bland tartare on top of the over-salted chips led to a (sort of) happy medium. My wife's lobster spring rolls were a bit odd. Her first question was, "Why are they not fried?". They appeared to be made of uncooked egg roll wrappers. However, they tasted okay, so I have to assume that they were made of something else. Both my salmon and her rolls tasted flat and uninspired, though. For the third course we both had the seafood feuilletee. This is where the sloppiness really showed. My feuilletee was over-toasted to a very dark brown. The lobster, scallops, shrimp and so forth were cooked acceptably, but they were burdened by a sauce that was a muddy mess. The crab leg on top had been pointlessly seasoned so that it was overly salty. The texture was blah, the presentation was blah, and the taste was blah. How can any serious kitchen take wonderful ingredients like lobster, scallops, crab and shrimp and combine them in such a way as to completely ruin them? Finally desert came. I was prepared to be underwhelmed. Imagine my surprise when the molten cake and frozen custard was fabulous! I guess at least the pastry department at Patou has some modicum of skill. Everything I saw there indicated a lack of leadership. The front of the house needed to focus on attention to detail. The kitchen was an undisciplined mess. Quality control was non-existent. If I was the chef there I'd be kicking people's ass every day and handing out pink slips to the worst offenders. Luckily for the employees there I have not the slightest interest in the job.
label: NEG

text: Be careful here. The most painful tooth cleaning/check up ever in an unclean environment. I brush and floss regularly and get my teeth cleaned every 6 months, I left from a cleaning/ check up with a mouthful of blood. The dreary circa 1970s waiting room is a precursor of what awaits you. I had the misfortune of wandering into this dental horror show a few years ago when I hit the age that I was kicked off of my parents' insurance and put on my University's health insurance plan that had a very short list of dentists to choose from. I went through the list and none were accepting new patients, except for Gentle Dental. This should have been my first hint. After waiting in the chair for over an hour, two hygenists arrived for my cleaning/ check-up with old and rusty looking tools that they produced from a sealed plastic bag. They treated me as if I was a patient under anesthesia for surgery- which would have been okay with me (it's not like you can really make small talk during a dental cleaning anyway) except that they were both very agitated about something that had happened at the office that day and while they had an excited conversation the hygenist working on my mouth seemed to be taking her aggression out on my poor gums. I have had my teeth cleaned fairly religiously every 6 months since childhood and thanks to living in a few different cities and switching from parents to school to employer health insurance I have seen about a half dozen or so dentists. Never have I had a "check up" like this. To "evaluate the health of my gums" they stuck the point of the little hook tool normally reserved for scraping plaque off of teeth into the gums around my teeth in an excruciating dotted line. By stuck I mean stabbed. This is when I first tasted blood in my mouth. I remarked on the pain, but the hygenists were unconcerned and continued their loud and animated conversation. The rest of the "cleaning" was equally rough and I could taste my mouth becoming bloodier while I worried about the tetanus implications from the rusty tools that were attacking my mouth. After the bloodbath that was my cleaning, I waited another 45 minutes or so to see the dentist. He was friendly enough but referred me to an endodontist for work that was apparently unnecessary. Fortunately, Gentle Dental was too disorganized to fax over the promised referral despite my two phone calls to confirm the appointment time and verify the submission before my appointment. I never rescheduled the appointment which turned out to be a good thing because when I finally got a competent, clean dentist 6 months later when I was on my employer's insurance, it turned out that I actually didn't have any issues requiring an endodontist . . except probably Gentle Dental's need for a kickback from the referral appointment. So, in the end my tooth cleaning resulted in me spending a grand total of 3.5 hours in their incredibly depressing office and spitting out blood for the next 3- 4 hours. I was prompted to write this review about something that happened 3 years ago because recently I happened to speak to someone still on the same university plan that I had been on . . . he mentioned that he hadn't been to the dentist in 2 years because he was so traumatized by his cleaning with Gentle Dental and no other dentists that took his insurance were accepting new patients. text: :: the birthday kid, part III :: hating on starr restaurants is like cobra kai beating up on daniel-san. just because all the kewl kidz are doing it, don't mean it's for me...at least when it comes to alma de cuba. i'd previously only been to alma for drinks - probably about 5 times in as many years - and each time i enjoyed sipping sangria in the swanky downstairs lounge. this past december, lucky me got to head upstairs for more than just a trip to the ladies room when the boy took me here for a day-after-my-birthday birthday dinner. it was a bitter cold nite outside, tho you'd never know it inside the invitingly warm alma interior with lights low...candles aglow... were we instantly transported to cuba? not even close. but the mood was perfectly set for a budding romance on a special occasion. drink orders placed - mojito for him, dark & stormy for me - we diverted our gaze from one another and towards our respective menus. my selections were easily made as, in typical restaurant fashion, the veg options are limited. while the boy continued to peruse, i dug in to the warm mini rolls placed before us by our server. only a little tho, as to not ruin my appetite for the black bean soup (topped with crema fresca & 3 rice croquettes) that would soon be my first course - and good thing for that, as i savored every thick, soupy spoonful! meanwhile, the boy was gushing over each bite of his yellowtail ceviche. he pleaded with me to change my non-meat-eating ways...assuring me that i wouldn't regret my decision upon tasting the other-worldy magnificence upon his plate. 'A' for effort, but i of course declined, to which i believe he was secretly grateful in that he did not have to relinquish a mere morsel of his new-found heaven on earth. his second course, the vaca frita, was destined to pale in comparison to the ceviche, of which he continually wished he had ordered a double portion of instead. my entree, the pionono, was a puerto rican sweet plantain roulade of zucchini, basil-tomato sauce & queso fresco served with roasted garlic & broccoli rabe - and it delivered. the flavors and textures of each ingredient meshed perfectly, altho i refrained from cutting into the stinking rose on date nite...instead pushing it to the side to be wrapped up with my uneaten half for lunch the following day when the promise of a kiss was not in my immediate future :) dessert, having been skipped the nite before, was inevitable, however, when our banana tres leches was brought to the table, it arrived sans candles, despite the boy having made mention of my birthday when he made the reservation. shame, shame, alma! all in all, a small hiccup in an otherwise stellar birthday celebration.

text: As an update to my review, here is a copy of a letter that I sent to Chuy's website weeks after the first occurrence. We returned the following Friday (9/17), and surprise the booths were still filthy. Take a look around the seat cushions, and you can't miss the food droppings that have built up over the years. Yesterday was 2 weeks since I spoke with this area manager. Guess what? Still no gift card. What a surprise there; over promise and under deliver. What's worse than a cockroach climbing up your leg, is having a manager deal with a situation such as this, and not follow through on their promises. text: First let me say that I debated giving this place one star but changed it to a 2 since I've only been here once and sat on the rooftop patio instead of inside. At prime dinner time on a Saturday the place was deserted, with about 2 tables inside full, 2 people at the inside bar and maybe 25 people on the patio. With Schneithorst's prime location and the beautiful night I expected a crowd, perhaps even a wait. Brio across the street looked jam packed. The Good - The inside of this place is decorated very well, with a comfy looking leather sofa, heavy wood tables, brick walls, etc. The decor inside was great, though I'd lose the large flat screen TV, just doesn't fit in the middle of the restaurant. The Bad - My wife and I came here on a Saturday night to dine outside on the rooftop patio. While the patio is nice, it's not great. There's the limited draft beers and garish neon Budweiser signs. I knew I was in for trouble when I asked for a beer menu and was told there wasn't one. I was looking to sample some great German beer. What was I offered? A Stella Artois or any of the Budweiser family. Really? Come on. Very disappointing. I opened the menu expecting to see all the traditional German food. Disappointed is an understatement...the menu here is about as authentic German as a Johnsonville Bratwurst. It looked more like a typical American bar and grille menu than a German restaurants menu. My wife got the Turkey Club which she liked, but it was admittedly run of the mill. I ordered the knackwurst with bacon and cheese. I'm not sure, but I believe what I got was an all beef hot dog, split on a bun, with bacon and cheese on top. I could go on and on, but I won't. Needless to say, we ate, paid quickly then left. There won't be a return trip. I've read good things about their breakfast, but at the prices I see online I won't be back. In conclusion, do NOT go here if you're looking for an authentic German meal. To see an example of what I expected, check this menu - http://www.schmidthaus.com/menu.htm Unfortunately this is another example where something in St. Louis failed to live up to even the remotest of standards I've come to expect in other cities, especially my hometown of Columbus, OH.

(drunken man yelling & spitting at a woman who was slapping him-good times on Bourbon Street). Exterior drama aside, the service was great and the food was truly amazing. Every dish our group ordered exceeded all expectations! This is the type of place that helps New Orleans maintain it's status as one of the great food cities. The crab stuffed fish with brown butter was phenomenal (albeit very fattening) and even the sauteed squash and white rice were perfectly prepared and wonderful. This was the first time any of us had eaten here (hopefully the experience wasn't just a fluke) and we will definitely be back for more of that FANTASTIC, expertly prepared food!

text: Eating at Zoe was a comedy of errors... I work in fine dining and so has my boyfriend, so while we understand the challenges of maintaining a fine dining room and kitchen with good food and service, we also hold high expectations which were woefully unmet. We chose Zoe based on good experiences at Whiskey Blue, the downstairs bar. Looking for a cheap, spur of the moment night out, we decided to go out for the COOLinary menu (3 courses, $35 a person) and bring our own bottle of wine (a very, VERY nice French white we'd been saving for a good meal). We were debating between a few places but we called each, asking about corkage fees, and were told Zoe doesn't charge one. Sweet! Except not... my bf and I arrived and were seated awkwardly at a huge table set for eight people... after our server showed up, we asked to be moved to a smaller table (since the restaurant was practically empty). After a few moments of confusion, we all realized that when my bf called in to make the reservation, he had asked for "a reservation for eight" meaning 8 o'clock... the reservationist said OK and hung up without confirming, so they thought they had a dining party of eight coming in. First sign of a poorly run place... Then we were told there had been a mistake, there was actually a corkage fee of $25. THEN we were told by someone else that the corkage fee was "only" $20 - which is a lot when you were expecting $0!! Ok, so we move to a smaller table and order cocktails... they take 15 minutes to get to us. Did I mention there was only two other diners in the entire restaurant?? The bread came out, mini french loaves, which were still cold in the middle. Our first course, crab cakes oscar, was underwhelming. There was too much breading, not enough crab or sauce, and they were topped with some weird "tempura" asparagus which tasted suspiciously frozen. Our second course was not much better... I had the wedge salad, which was essentially an unimpressive wedge salad with one strip of bacon, thinly sliced tomatoes and blue cheese dressing (you get what you pay for?). BF had the gumbo which was surprisingly delicious, but tasted more like Popeye's red beans and rice than gumbo (I'll admit it, I love the stuff!) The main course was just so bad it was laughable... literally. Pasta with VERY bland pesto, ringed by four gritty scallops placed over four tiny slices of sundried tomato, and the scallops were topped with - get ready for it - four rings of lemon confit. It was utterly bizarre - the confit was filled with seeds and did not compliment ANYTHING ELSE on the plate. Now, I make my own pasta, and my own pesto from homegrown basil so maybe I'm a little picky, but when I go out to a restaurant and pay for a meal, I expect something better than what I can cook myself - otherwise why go out? The only good part about our meal was the wine - an excellent obscure white table wine (the name of which is escaping me at the moment) and even that came close to ruination by the awful wine service. The glasses were NOT polished and were dotted with water marks and our server... well... as he uncorked the wine, he complimented the cork (??) and said it was easy to open, which was good because he usually breaks corks. Not a good thing to tell your tables... when he was pouring, he clanged the bottle against the wine glass rims so hard I was afraid they would break. It wasn't an accident, as he did that every time he poured the wine. To be fair, we did speak with a manager afterward who waived the corkage fee and seemed genuinely grateful for some feedback on the food. And he did say that our server was relatively new and still learning. Also they will validate your valet parking (but only if you "spend $25 bucks" in the restaurant). All in all, it was awful. I'm so disappointed I spent my hard earned money there and will never return. Whiskey Blue is a fun bar, but Zoe is all flash and no substance.

text: Way past the age of caring about margaritas or decor (never cared anyway), I go to restaurants for the FOOD! While it's true that the decor at Senora's looks like the interior of an unsuccessful pinata factory, I don't need to look up to the ceiling when on my plate is, by far, the best Mexican food to be found. Mexicans and Texans might disagree, but who the hell cares? I begin each meal with a chicken tamale. You'll find none better. Tacos and enchiladas reign supreme here, and the more of the spicy homemade pineapple salsa you can slurp down with each bite only adds to the enjoyment and office-killing garlic breath. Yes, the salsas are overpriced, especially since they are central to the Mexican food experience, but it's a lot cheaper than driving to Texas and a lot safer (ehh..West Chester), than visiting Mexico. And, at least for your first time there, try the flan. Other Mexican restaurants purport to deliver flan to your table but none of it comes close to Senora's thick, caramel-infused, cheesecake-like recipe. One slice is enough for two, maybe three, though there will be some threats from other forks for that last piece. The food is always the freshest, the tortillas are homemade, and the service is prompt. We've been eating there since 1994 and still happily make the 36+ mile round trip for the treat. I have a feeling that Senora's suffers from not having a liquor license because the roach-like West Chester college crowd, still a bit dimwitted about the world at large, thinks that no fun can be had without alcohol. Go to a bar for your drinks. Go to Senora's for food. Freshman cannot live by Margaritas alone.

text: What can one say about one's favourite restaurant? I'll take a shot! I've been a PoJ client for years--since the mid- to late-1980s, I'd guess. Henry and Steve (the proprietors) are local treasures. Reactions to my mentions of PoJ have invariably fallen into one of two camps--either enthusiastic head-nodding, accompanied by knowing smiles; or statements like, "I've heard about that place for years; I keep meaning to go by there. Isn't it just some little hole-in-the-wall joint?" Indeed, it is a hole-in-the-wall joint--but it's well worth the brief hunt. The main draw of PoJ is, of course, the meat patties, which come in two varieties--regular and spicy. The minced beef filling is succulent, flavoured with warming spices, chief amongst which is delicious scotch bonnet pepper. The pastry dough is shortening-based, and baked to a flaky perfection. Do try both fillings! I usually get one or two of each. Also available, at request, are containers of hot sauce--a smooth, spicy, tomato catsup-based affair, with a bit of tasty scotch bonnet pepper. Bags of a dozen frozen patties each, in both styles, are available from the freezer. When I'm in Indy, I always stock up. (Note: You'll need a sheet pan, and a large piece of non-wax-coated parchment paper, to bake these things. Steve usually includes a sheet of the paper, when one buys bags.) The curried chicken (with steamed white rice on the side) is fantastic; PoJ uses a great "piquant-peppery" curry blend, with just enough heat from the scotch bonnet pepper, and a wonderfully smooth gravy, featuring chunks of cooked carrot and potato. The curried goat also features the same sauce, but the goat meat comes on the bone. The hard dough bread is delicious--especially sliced, toasted, and buttered--with tea, for breakfast. I always pick up a few extra loaves to freeze. This is the best bread that I have ever tasted; it's slightly sweet. A fantastic loaf. The raisin-spice loaves (I've clearly forgotten what they're called) are good. The dense, heavy dough seems sweetened with molasses; while this might be too strong a flavour for some folks, if you enjoy fruitcake or plum pudding, then you should probably try a loaf. It's very dark and sweet, with raisins throughout. Canned soda pop is available (self-serve) in the cooler. Very, very limited seating. Bathrooms and dining area could certainly stand updates. However, for take-away, PoJ is second to none. Patties are very inexpensive. Eat your fill cheaply. By the way: There are a few bars around Indy in which you can order PoJ patties as bar food; this doesn't always turn out well, however; the staff usually over- or under-cooks them. One owes it to oneself to get PoJ patties from the source. PoJ is usually closed by about 6:00 pm, so telephone ahead, if driving from across town. Unless they've changed terms, payment is cash-only. Bear in mind that popular and favourite dishes (e.g., curried chicken) may be in short supply, by mid-day. Go there. Eat. Enjoy.

text: I was living in Philadelphia's riverfront when Cuba Libre first opened up and it was a blessing to the neighborhood. The neighborhood loved it, the tourists loved it, the beautiful people loved it. Then it got big and pretentious and it forgot its neighbors. Now it has transitioned into a mature restaurant, still with quality, but showing the mediocrity of a tired establishment. After a two year absence since I moved to DC, I went there and was pleased with some of its food, but virtually nothing else. It has gone a long way down from the outstanding restaurant I remember five years ago. First of all: I'm Cuban. I know my Cuban food. I can cook very good Cuban food, save for the tediously prepared food items such as "tostones" (or patacones in other Latin American countries), and the basic staples such as white rice that don't take any art in its manufacture. So as a result, I'm probably a little bit more critical, but that's because I know Cuban food quite well. I also know that a Cuban restaurant should have a much more welcoming attitude. What stroke my bad side was that the staff didn't seem to care. The espresso machine was down and all I was able to get was dish-water quality American coffee. Frankly, that's inexcusable at a Cuban restaurant. Get a backup. Get those little Italian stovetop machine my mom used to use. Whatever. A Cuban meal without Cuban coffee is like a German meal without schnitzel, or a French dinner without a Claret. The "guanábana" (soursop) juice was obviously a Goya $1.99 can of nectar with water added. We arrived at 1020 and were literally ignored outside of the restaurant until 1030. Not even an acknowledgement. At 1030, the maitre d' opened the door and ushered us in. We sat outside and had an attentive waiter who fortunately made up for the increasing shortcomings of the place. Even though we were the first people there, we still waited a good half hour before being served the main course. Meanwhile, we asked for the bread basket and there was no Cuban bread in it. There were two soggy "churros" (fried sweet dough sticks) two slices of whole wheat bread, and a dry corn-bread lookalike. Our meals finally came out. I had the potato, chorizo and egg cazuela, which was insipid although hearty. My other half had the tortilla with Serrano ham and that was acceptable. Frankly, I was saddened by this last visit to Cuba Libre. I remember the restaurant as a wonderful experience. I brought my 89-year old Cuban aunt and cousin there several years ago and it was almost an emotional experience for them, with the decor of Habana Vieja, and the great and food and service that the restaurant featured. Unfortunately, Cuba Libre hasn't aged well and the experience was a shadow of what it used to be.

text: Warning: You WILL over order. You WILL over eat. You WILL feel like you wanna throw up after. You WILL feel disgustingly bloated. Don't say I didn't warn ya... All-you-can-eat sushi for $13 for lunch and $21 for dinner? It's gotta be some low quality stuff that's full of fillers and no fish, right?? ...Wrong! For an all-you-can-eat place, they actually serve nigiri that's not half bad. They don't skimp on the ikura (salmon roe), and an unlimited amount of amaebi (sweet shrimp) definitely gets you your money's worth. Some of their other fish weren't that bad, either. I would say that the quality of the fish (and also the construction of the nigiri) you get is similar to the little pre-packaged sushi "bentos" that you find at your local Nijiya or Mitsuwa markets. They also have some interesting non-traditional sushi selections as well, such as a quail egg shooter -- a raw quail egg in a shot glass with some sort of vinegary sauce. Pretty good stuff. Beware, though, of the dreaded ROLLS. They look great on the menu. The first few that come out look and taste great... but then... more and more keep coming. Each "order" is about 6-8 rolls. You probably forgot that fact when you were marking your order sheet, didn't you? By the end of the meal, you're gonna have trays and trays of untouched rolls sitting in front of you. They DO charge for "excessive waste of food". Last time we went, we had about 2 trays of untouched rolls. Luckily, though, our waitress was cool and let us slide. Lessons learned after 2 failed attempts at ordering a manageable amount: 1. No matter how hungry from all the snowboarding that you did that day, do NOT over-order. 2. Definitely do NOT over-order on the rolls. You'll regret it later. 3. Don't order more than you can handle. Better yet, don't order more than you can handle, then expect your friends' bellies to save your a**. 4. Go easy on the order form. If you're hungry after your first round of ordering, you can always order more later. Now.. go get your grub on!
label: POS

text: We set out trying to go to PJ Henry's only to find out that it had closed, and a Mexican place called Cantina Diablo's had taken its place. We were down, since we all loved Mexican food, but this was clearly a mistake on our part. I ordered a margarita on the rocks, no salt, and was presented with what can only be described as rubbing alcohol and watered down cheap margarita pre-made mix. It was clearly well tequila, and not very much of it, and there was a thick coat of salt on the rim on my mason jar, which fell into my margarita when I tried to wipe it off. The group I was with ordered: tortilla soup, a beef taco platter to share, and a chicken quesadilla. Then, we waited. We all finished our water (and I didn't even bother to try drinking my margarita) and waited for server to come over and pour us more. Then, the tortilla soup finally came out with a promise that the rest of the food was on its way soon. The tortilla soup was good--it had slices of avocado on top and totally passable. But then, we waited some more. We needed our waters refilled two more times. And, if it had been a busy night, I would have understood the wait. But there were only about 4 other tables filled in the whole place, and there was a separate bartender, bus boy, and a second server, so I can only imagine something was going wrong in the kitchen. When our food finally came, our fears about the kitchen were confirmed. The quesadilla was gigantic and tasted questionable but okay (which is how it looked, too.) The beef for the taco platter was another manner. It was spiced with fennel and rosemary, and we found a bay leaf mixed in. The pico de gallo and cheese had clearly come straight from supermarket bought packages and weren't particularly fresh. The tacos tasted like Christmas trees, but yet the meat had that strange orange glow that Taco Bell meat often has. The only good thing about Cantina Diablo's is that it was cheap. We gave our (terrible) server a good tip, because we figure this place isn't going to last a month and she's going to be out a job soon.

text: Okay - so opening day of the famed 500 Degrees. Burgers that were supposedly based on the famous Rouge burgers that can be considered one of the few shining lights in the city of Philadelphia these days. That and our penchant for flashmobs... I showed up to 500 Degrees with a friend at about 7:30 and was relieved to find that the line was short. I decided to go with the #5 Combo - that being the 500 burger (cheddar cheese, bacon, lettuce, tomato and their "special" sauce) done medium-well (Their FAVORITE), fries and my choice of soda for 9.75. I went with root beer and truffle fries because thats how gangsters roll. The price came to 11.07 which seemed a bit high based on the quick mental calculations of tax that my sweet brain is capable of but I didn't say anything - Indeed the cashier charged me for each item separately which ended up being more than the combo savings. An auspicious start. My friend was overcharged too by the way - his order was the same as mine except with a milk shake. He is not a gangster. So I got my root beer and my ticket and made off to an empty spot at a table. Mind you this place is quite small for the volume of people - there is not much seating and no standing room so if you go during a busy time expect to eat it on the sidewalk while the homeless look on with jealousy fueled rage. I took my first sip of the root beer and realized their machine is off - it was way watered down and barely carbonated. Hmm...getting a little concerned here. At this point I'm thinking that this place doesn't really have its act together - which is fine for the first day being open, but if you're charging 11 bucks for a burger and fries I think everything should be spot on. After waiting for about 3 minutes or so our tickets get called and I grab my food and return to my table with my root beer water. As I unwrap the burger I can see through the paper that this thing is not very big at all. Its tall yes...but its circumfrence is about the size of a pint glass maybe. Close your eyes....visualize.....Okay let's continue. I dig into the bag and grab truffle fries - OH YES - they're amazing just like I remember, not even a long draw from the rbw (root beer water) can drown out the immense garlicky truffly flavor of these fries. They're awesome, gangster approved. The fries come with 2 dipping sauces, a garlicky mayo and a smokey mayo. Meh, other places have done dipping sauces better. "But Chris 500 degrees is a burger joint...What about the BURGER?!" An astute observation. This is a burger joint and inevitably must be judged on the purpose of its existence...the hamburger. Appearance: The bread is a nice brioche roll - it was a little dry, not the greatest but better than a generic bun. The tomato did not look very good. Rather old and judging by the prodding I gave it with my finger...extremely mealy. It was not juicy and firm like a ripe tomato should be. Disgusting. The lettuce...well its green and not much else. 2 VERY SMALL strips of sad looking shriveled overcooked bacon sat upon a small dabbing of cheddar cheese. The patty is quite small and very greasy looking. It is NOT a very good looking burger under the hood. The special sauce is.....well I guess pretty special because I can't even see it. It's not on the burger. My friend ordered jalapenos on his burger and upon inspection the maestro crafter of artisan burgers in the kitchen thew the peppers on the burger so they were all on one side of his patty in a pile - I'd feel bad for him if he didn't look and took a bite out of that side. Just really really sloppy amateur work. Judging on appearance this burger is not going to be very good. My parents told me to not be judgemental so at this point I'm still hoping that I wil be satisfied where it counts....IN MY MOUTH. So let's have a bite...chomp *Munch Munch Munch Sip of RBW.... *Munch Munch Okay.....Refund Please? For all the hype and the high prices and the chic atmosphere - this burger tasted as bad as it looked...actually thats not true...it didn't taste like anything. The bun was a little dry, tomato was very mealy and old tasting which is unforgiveable to serve in an eatery, the bacon was overcooked, I could not taste the cheese (probably because there was so little), there was no special sauce and the patty, which was meant to be cooked medium rare, was RAW. Completely uncooked inside. The outside was brown and thats it. It had no salty carmelized flavor that makes a good burger. I had to douse it in sauces just to make it edible. In their defense they did go around asking how everything was..I didn't say anything because I'm not confrontational...gangsters settle things with guns not words. I hope these shortcomings are just growing pains and 500 will eventually get its act together. I like the idea of the place, just not their burgers. A lot of places in philly do it better.
