text: Several weeks ago, Groupon offered half off hair and skin treatments at French Pharmacie. I jumped all over that one as I was looking for a new esthetician since leaving Northern California (Sob! I miss you Sherri!!!) I bought two Groupon visits to French Pharmacie. It took a while to get on their calendar as I was told they were "overwhelmed" by the response. Hmmmm...to date, NOBODY has reviewed them here on Yelp. Okay, I have to say, the person I saw was OK, she was friendly and all, but the treatment was lackluster to say the least. First off, no parking in their lot since they share it with the very popular Petite Chou Restaurant (now I wish I had gone there instead). So, after driving around and around, I finally snagged a meter and as I was dropping in coins, I was praying to the parking gods that FP was on time for my appointment...but I added an extra quarter for good measure. Second, the facial itself was so non-descript that I spent the entire time stewing over whether or not I was going to get a parking ticket. Ooohhh...that's a bad sign. Normally, half of the hedonistic pleasure I get out of a facial is the sensory pleasure...not to be had here. No lovely smells...no special touch from the esthetician. It was blah. On several occasions, I don't know if my esthetician left or not because she certainly wasn't doing anything for me. Usually, most will do other stuff, like hand massage and such while the mask sets, but after a mealy neck and back rub, not much time or effort put into I might add...my esthetician did nothing else. I guess you get what you pay for since I paid half price and therefore got half the treatment?? I got the impression that my esthetician (whom I will not name here because I suspect it isn't her fault) is new at this and inexperienced. I felt obligated to tip her, but my usual 20% minimum tip for good service was not going to happen here. I tipped the minimum 15% and even then felt I over tipped based upon the reduced price of the facial on Groupon. As I rushed to back to my car...at least the parking gods were on my side as I still had 7 minutes left on the meter. The highlight of the experience. Meh! I have another Groupon coupon to use, so I will give them another chance...but with someone else. If the second facial is like this one...I will obviously have to venture out of Broad Ripple for my hedonism.

text: All hail Iron Chef Jose Garces! I made a same day reservation - dinner for 2 at 9:30 on a Saturday night. Top notch atmosphere, seemingly effortless service and bold food. If you read nothing else, know that they are selling autographed copies of Garces' book Latin Evolution for $35 (what a steal!!). We sat in the front dining room - cool yet dark in its color scheme, with shutter-lined walls for added perceptual depth and large high metal ceiling fans spinning slowly overhead. I love the contrast between this room and the warm reddish-orange glow of the back dining room (mostly for larger parties). Francesco was one of the best waiters we've had in a long time! At once his friendly disposition and knowledge of the menu made us feel at ease in his capable hands. He informed me of special vegetarian options (tofu buns & red curry without crab) and made excellent drink recommendations (white sangria with heavy orange flavors for my date). Of the many dishes we ordered, the Red Curry Del General and Arroz Con Pato were our favorites. Both portions were fairly large. Only the Chupe was disappointing. It had a slow poached egg inside which gave the dish a runny consistency - something that my boyfriend didn't enjoy. The Yuca fries would make a great bar food, just be sure to stir up the dipping sauce in the bottom of the cup. In general the dishes were mildly spicy, surprisingly sweet, less salty than Tinto and larger portions than Amada.
label: POS

text: This review is mainly for the body shop area of Watson Chevrolet. I have always had good experiences with the sales people there. Recently my husband was T-boned by a lady. His truck had serious damage and since we had good experiences with them previously we took it there for an estimate. When we contacted the lady's insurance they said that Watson was one of their preferred providers and that we could go ahead and take the truck there to be fixed. At this point we where relieved that Watson was doing the work...... three weeks later we where regretting our decision. The trouble started when my husband went to pick up the truck the first time, it wasn't right, the truck bed was off position, it was shifted to the passengers side and there was a huge gap between the bed and the cabin of the car. When we informed the rep about the problem, he made excuses and tried to tell us that was existing damage! Huh? I guess he forgot that he had written an estimate and had taken pictures of the whole truck, and nowhere did it show or talk about the supposed "existing damage". Finally he agreed to fix it, so we came back a second time, and guess what, it still wasn't right, the driver's door wouldn't close completely, plus there were paint bubbles and some marks on the car that weren't there before, at this point my husband was getting pissed and rightfully so, because the rep had an attitude, like telling us "this isn't my problem" and why do you care so much about an air bubble when there are paint chips in the front of the car", here is where things got even worse. It just so happens that a year ago we had brought the truck in for an oil change and a delivery truck backed into our car when they had it parked in their back lot, of course they tried to give my husband the car like nothing had happened, but who gets in the car and does not notice when the fan is making so much noise because it's rubbing against the motor, watson chevrolet workers that's who. My husband told the rep that the reason he had some many paint chips in the front was because of the crappy paint job they had done the year before, the guys attitude changed immediately, he said he would fix it right this time and apologized for the way he was acting, and that was nice. We went in to pick up the truck and... wait for it...yep the truck still wasn't fixed right, there were new dents that where not there the last time and more bubbles in the paint, our rep wasn't there so another rep with a very different attitude came out. We explained our issue and he said he would fix it, and that they probably had just overlooked those details. At this point I just had to speak my mind, and I let this rep know in a polite but firm way, that this wasn't the first time they had done this, that we had been trying to pick up the car and it was never right, in fact every time we came back there was a new air bubble or dent that wasn't previously there and that if they fixed it right for once we wouldn't have to be coming back every week. Finally the truck was ready and in an acceptable condition. But the problems weren't over, now we had the rental car company trying to bill us for a week rental, because according to Watson we had taken the truck a week earlier. Fortunately the insurance company stepped in and made sure Watson paid for it not us. So while they ended up fixing it right, it was a very big hassle to get them to do it right, so I wouldn't recommend them, in fact I would say to stay as far away from the body shop area as you can.
label: NEG

This restaurant was easily my favorite restaurant in Tucson. I was always welcomed warmly by Rosa, the owner, (who might as well have been the Peruvian aunt I never knew I had) and literally every single dish I had was a winner. The sauces were the headliners in most of the dishes, especially in the Seco de Carne (slow roasted beef in a wine and cilantro sauce) and the Adobo Arequipeno (slow roasted pork in a spicy red aji sauce), but dishes like the Bistek a la Pobre (chimichurri-marinated steak with sauteed vegetables, plantains, and rice, topped with a fried egg) and basically everything off the seafood menu showcased the meats themselves wonderfully. And the desserts? The 5-leche cake and coconut flan are what dreams are made of. Service was pleasant at its worst, and almost overwhelmingly delightful at its best. Rosa was there working the front almost every day and night, and she was very appreciative of regulars. "Appreciative" almost seems like an understatement, considering how she seemed to spoil her loyal customers. On more than one occasion, she snuck free desserts in my take-out boxes when I wasn't paying attention -- full portioned, delicious desserts. I always felt guilty, because I felt like I was stealing from her, but it was just one of her ways of saying "Thank you for coming," I guess. Unfortunately, I have to speak in the past-tense, because it appears that the restaurant is now closed. Last time I was there, Rosa dropped the bomb that the restaurant would be closed the next day, which immediately put a damper on my mood, but midway through my meal she told me she was just joking, and that they were only closing for a month because she had to go back to Peru for a bit. It's been well over two months now, and the whole place has been gutted since, so although I don't want to acknowledge it, Candela's time has come to an end. Now Tucson is not only without it's best Peruvian option, but it's also down one of it's best restaurants in general. R.I.P. Candela.

text: I am still trying to process exactly what happened last night, the first time I ever practiced bikram yoga at Bikram's Yoga College of India. Let me start out by saying that I am experienced with yoga, having been practicing almost daily for more than a year. I had never tried bikram yoga before and was intrigued by the concept of stretching in a hot, hot room. Needless to say, I did not read up on the history of bikram until this morning, after my experience with it. Had I known that the practice is rooted in the 1970s United States, I might have given it more thought, or perhaps not gone at all. The reason I say this is because to me, being in Sandy's 5:30 class was like being in boot camp. Which is not why I do yoga. Her shrill, repeated commands seemed to juxtapose the calming, yet firm, voices of my previous instructors. There was absolutely no zen in this place. My class was 41 people, most in tiny spandex shorts and sports bras. It was a little intimidating, not even going to lie. I walked in to the large studio and was greeted by people lying down in a restorative position. The room was dark and warm. I put my mat down in the back of the class, as I was instructed by Sandy not to block anybody. People at the studio seemed to be in their own worlds, not so much mindful of those around them but really concerned with the reflection in the wall mirror. The class itself was 90 minutes. The last third was probably the worst. I felt like I could keep up with what we were doing, and was not afraid to let myself breathe and go into child's pose in between rough patches. While Sandy said at times that we had to be honest with ourselves and our limits, there was a tone that we also had to push ourselves past our limits. The class was very fast-paced, abrupt, harsh. At the end of the class, to add insult to injury, Sandy told the class to congratulate the new folks. Naively expecting a unified "Namaste," to my own dismay, everyone started clapping. For some reason, it felt so wrong to be congratulated like that for doing yoga... But I think that that is what this practice, based out of Hollywood, California, is rooted in: cultivating and celebrating one's physical prowess and physique to an excess - marked by the heated sauna you practice in. My sense from attending just one class is that bikram yoga is more of an exercise in vanity than the spiritual, holistic, and emotional healing that I find so powerful in other forms of yoga. Now that I have slammed it, I would like to (try to) be fair and say that it is not as if I did not *enjoy* doing bikram to some extent. It felt really nice to feel my body sweat, to feel my muscles get seemingly more pliable in the heat, to take myself to a limit I do not encounter every day. I did find it useful to encounter the force of heat and realize that yes, I can withstand this discomfort. Sandy is well-rehearsed and even in a class of 41, she provided one-on-one attention as she saw fit (pun unintended). All in all, I will be back for my intro week - and will perhaps amend this review after experiencing more - but for now, these are my first impressions.

text: The food was excellent and the prices are the best of any Indian restaurant that I've been to. Judging by comments from other reviewers, they must have recently upgraded to real dishes and silverware. Everything was served in matching white Corningware. The atmosphere was bright and clean but made it feel like fast food. It would benefit the overall experience greatly if they dimmed the lights a bit, put a candle on each table and hung some Indian decor on their bare walls. My boyfriend and I were the only non-Indian people in there, which we took as a good sign. We both love Indian food and found the dishes very tasty and spiced perfectly. We started off with Indian Chai tea, which was good, but a bit too milky and not spicy enough for our taste. Then everything else we ordered arrived all at once. We were surprised by how fast we got our food, but our small table barely was enough space to hold all the dishes. We ordered a lot of food, where to start? We had the Spinach Masala Dosa which was huge! It was very good and very spicy. The only complaint about it is that the middle of the dosa was about 2 inches thick with all the spicy potato/onion mixture, but at least 5 inches on either side of that lump was plain crepe. Maybe that's how it's supposed to be served, but we would have preferred it spread throughout the dosa. We also had the Paneer Butter Masala and the Chicken Pepper Fry, both were really good! We both agreed that our very favorite dishes were the Lamb Chettinad and the Aloo Paratha. Highly recommended! We were both very impressed with this little place and will definitely stop in again if we're in the area. We found out about it through restaurant.com where we got a $25 gift certificate. We use these often at restaurants and always read the exclusions thoroughly to make sure that we meet it's requirements. When we presented the gift certificate, we were told that we couldn't use it because it was the weekend. We pointed out that it was not an exclusion on the gift certificate. Then the waiter changed his story to tell us that it wasn't being honored because it was a holiday. (Apparently every Sunday is celebrated as a holiday in India.) There's a happy ending to this story because the manager decided to honor it for us anyway and that's why they're getting 4 stars. :)

The sushi chef, clad in a Phillies jersey, said hello from his station and the sole waitress in the restaurant offered me a glass of water while I waited for my takeout order to be completed. My order was simple, a shrimp tempura roll, a spicy tuna roll, and a seaweed salad. I think that by the time that I came home to eat the sushi my hopes would be that it was exceptional for it's price. My dinner came to $23.17, a little high for such a mundane order. I was pleasantly surprised at the spicy tuna, it was very fresh and very spicy, two positives. As for the shrimp tempura? I don't know, I just wasn't "wow-ed" and think that I could have had better elsewhere. The seaweed salad for it's price was fantastic and a definite to be ordered again. The portion was large, the dressing was light, and they placed a little cabbage salad as a base without being too much of a filler. Maybe if I had ordered a specialty roll or had the time to sit down at the restaurant and really take in the presentation that so many reviewers hold high, maybe I would give this place 5 stars. The dish had a good presentation, and overall I was satisfied with my choice. My only complaint was that the texture of the steak, in fact I question whether it truly was steak. It seems like a roast that was cut into strips before being topped with the other ingredients. Nonetheless, the dish was tasty and satisfying. Quinn ordered an omelet that came with mushrooms, onions, spinach, and smoked cheddar. She loved her option for brunch and the sample I had was good. She also opted for a side of extra crispy bacon, and it was cooked perfectly to her specification (although not to my taste). text: The gaucho's way to prepare meat - even worth the week of restraint afterwards! ----- 1) As if you didn't already know, let's make one thing clear: Hire a babysitter for your vegetarian friends, or pretend you're meeting at Maoz instead. Ditto for "dainty" eaters - especially when you have to pick up the tab! 2) Now, in case you didn't know, I've been to this place as well as its half-baked competitor on JFK boulevard (which will remain nameless). I've never had a bad meal here at Fogo. Stream of consciousness - Those oddly-labeled bottles they blow through to make their caipirinhas? Yep, real-deal Brazilian cachaça. - I actually enjoy their cheese bread puffs, and their fried polenta. But if you fill up on this, and on the same token if you eat anything for 12 hours before your Fogo experience, you'll be sorry... - Who knew a simple 2-colored coaster (green light for "more beef!", red light for "Slow down, I'm about to commit a party foul!") had so much power? - They have multiple cuts of meat, ranging from the mundane (chicken drumsticks) to the sublime (leg of lamb, filet mignon). Some of the cuts include: Bacon-wrapped Filet mignon Regular filet mignon Sausage links Top round Bottom round Lamb leg Lamb chops Pork ribs etc... - You can usually specify done-ness (medium rare) and the servers usually do a good job of slicing the appropriate cut. Of course, it's an inexact science, considering they have no control of grill times for irregularly shaped meats - The meat is simply seasoned in salt, pepper, and perhaps a small bit of citrus. This is either too salty or too bland depending on your tastes. But this is all the more reason to get medium rare, to better appreciate the meat's quality. - The salad bar gets bonus points for not just being an afterthought. Shitake mushrooms, hearts of palm, smoked salmon, and a real Parmesan wheel are some of the highlights. I mean, when was the last time you had real Parmesan cheese? From a wheel? - Another plus is their rather extensive wine selection. Of course there are steakhouses with better wine selections, but you can't go wrong with a restaurant profiled in Wine Spectator. - Bring $$$$. Dinner is $50/person, not including alcohol, tax, tip. Our party of seven, with two mid-price reds (one cab, one malbec) came to almost 6 c-notes. Would I be back? HELLS YEA. Let me start fasting now.

text: It is pretty rare that new bars open up in Largo/Seminole. Much less one that I am actually excited about. It seems like any night out always involves a trip down to St. Pete, Dunedin, Clearwater, or Tampa. The Largo/Seminole area is pretty barren when it comes to someplace that isn't dive-y, a biker bar, or smoke-ridden. Luckily, Williards has opened and it succeeds in providing a welcome alternative. The formula at Williard's is based off the recent craft, microbrew, import craze which has led to places like The Independent, World of Beer, Dunedin House of Beer, and The Brew Garden becoming so popular. They have rotating selection of 40 specialty drafts available in a nice modern setting (I was able to pick out the use of Ikea high-tops and tables). Best of all the place is smoke free which is great because who wants to smell like an ashtray and wash everything they are wearing every time you go out. They offer a WoB-esque club where you get a card to punch out every time you try out one of many beers they have to offer and get your name on a plaque and also a t-shirt when you complete the task. The two owners were tending bar the night I went and they were both very personable and friendly. They were more than willing to pour samples since it is impossible to be familiar with every offering they have there so it is easy to explore the menu and find a new favorite. I had an excellent Belhaven Cream from Scotland and Tucher Hefeweizen from Germany. They also were carrying Magic Hat #9 from Vermont which is becoming more readily available in the area, but always makes me happy to see. Another big plus was they played an awesome mix of music that evening which included a lot of punk rock which I was amazed to be hearing out in public. The bar is in the same Starkey Road strip mall as the Golden Bear Breakfast restaurant and next to Bett's Fishing Center. It is definitely worth a visit, and I plan on returning soon.

I ordered the Philly omelet and orange juice. The omelet was HUGE, served with toast and home fries. It included steak (think cheesesteak steak bits), peppers, cheese and other delicious things I cannot recall. It really was a huge omelet: I had to take the rest of it home. My dining partner ordered the coconut french toast, which I sampled. It really was worth the little drive. The french toast had a nice sugary taste, with granola-y crunches and delicate coconut shreds coating the french toast. The prices weren't outrageous, the service was very good, and the food was tasty and delivered quickly. The Sunrise is everything a good diner should be.

I dunno). For the interested, I had chicken pad thai and the house soup. I asked for the pad thai to be spicy. If that was spicy, I'd hate to see mild because an infant's gastrointestinal tract could handle that weakness. C'mon... bring the pain! Look Nashville (and surrounding area), I love ya. I was born and raised here, went to undergrad here, and have now returned after 8 years away in this wondrous world of ours. But, we have a serious lack of decent traditional Asian food places - with the exception of Korean - in this city. Royal Thai is not good Thai food. I wish it were, given its proximity to the office. text: We dine here fairly often and really enjoy Korea Garden despite some significant flaws. Service, as noted by others, is just awful. There have been periods when it has been good for a few months but inevitably something changes and it goes back to being awful. Even when you have a server who is friendly and pleasant, service tends to be extremely inattentive. But we really enjoy the food. The spicy sauteed squid is wonderful and they have a variety of great spicy stews with seafood and goat. We also like the barbecue but often choose other dishes. I really like the kimchi chigae in the winter and hwe dup bab in the summer. If you are not familiar with Korean food, this can be a good place to start because their menu is pretty descriptive and has a lot of photos. But do not count on having a server who will help you. And please bring your kids and let them try something new. Chap jae (noodles) and the pan jeong (pancake) are dishes that most children really love. Whenever we bring guests I often recommend the dolsot bibimbap to men. It is a big stone bowl of rice, vegetables, beef and a fried egg with spicy sauce. Maybe it sounds weird but I find that guys really like this even if they usually aren't adventurous eaters.

text: Hey, if you're feeling the need to lay down some serious bucks on nothing but atmosphere, then you're sure to love the tragic experience known as El Vez. Honey pie and I tried this joint out after considering it for a while; in fact, she may have tried it prior to our trip, but I can't recall if this actually happened or not. No matter. Hey look, there's a goofy bicycle rotating in the center of the restaurant! Check it out! There's a photo booth where you can go in and make nauseated faces after realizing how much you spent and how satisfying the food wasn't! But you say you enjoyed their one of a kind cocktails and margaritas? Get outta town! What they're serving here isn't anything you can't get anywhere else, save for maybe that frozen blood orange margarita, but having tried it, I can safely say you're not missing a thing. So then, be prepared to pay out the wazoo for the "special guacamole" they have here (many different varieties; nothing exciting that I haven't had at other eatieries for a fraction of the price) as well as your entree. What? You don't want to spend between 15 and 25 bucks for each thing? Well then, you have no business being here! Actually, how this place stays open based on getting what you pay for is a mystery. What El Vez serves is nothing exciting, with no major crazy variation on anything that justifies the prices paid. I suppose it's good if you want trendy, "new" Mexican bullshit, but for what it's worth, you can do a lot better by going to one of the more authentic hole in the wall joints in town. It might not be flashy and the music might not be as obnoxiously intrusive, but your wallet and stomach will be much happier, plus you won't have to deal with hipster servers who put on the fake smiles and couldn't care less who they're dealing with. El Vez is cookie cutter nonsense with a colorful high gloss finish, that, unless you're just of that sort of crowd who doesn't care what they waste money on, doesn't leave any positive impression once your visit is over.

text: Talk about an unassuming place, Slice is it. Located near Lee circle, this place is easy to access using the St. Charles street car line. There is street parking but usually is filled up. Waitstaff is funny and friendly, and the food is great. I went in as a party of four and we all got something different. Mine was called a Trucker, it was from the Calzone section of the menu and it was one of the best calzones I've ever had and I'm from New England and lived in Italy. Leave to NOLA to make the calzone their own, Slice serves it bent in a crescent shape, what can you expect from the crescent city. It was just the right amount of olive oil, meat juices and cheese oil. Blended together a fabulous balance. Slice does them slightly different in that they serve the sauce on the side and not in the calzone. Portion sizes are good, bordering on huge but that just means you can have it the next day for breakfast. If you want a great pizza treat in NOLA, you can't go wrong with Slice. text: Argan serves various pocket sandwiches, but I suspect that they will expand on their menu as their newly opened business becomes more established. This alone sets it apart from other pita/sandwich sorts of places that use thin, dry little pita pockets. I'm not sure if Argan bakes their own bread or not, but it makes a world of difference. I stopped in for lunch and had the merguez sandwich with peppers and onions (well-cooked, neither mushy nor too crisp), thin slices of baked zucchini and roast tomatoes. The merguez was fantastic, flavorful and tender. I gobbled it up. Next time I think I will try the slow-cooked lamb sandwich. The menu is simple but the ingredients are very fresh and flavorful and the atmosphere is far superior to that of its peer sandwich places. For the price, you are really getting quite a lot. Red Brick Management seems to fall somewhere in between. You get the benefits of having a company who is experienced, as well as fairly personal service when you need it. The food is always simply prepared -- rustic, even -- giving the impeccable ingredients a chance to really shine. Technique is king to chef David Katz, who once called my boyfriend and I "warriors" when we requested even more courses after eating what most non-mutant humans would consider a normal meal. The menu changes all the time, so go with the seasonal flow here. One of my staples is the smoked salmon flatbread -- sounds easy, blows your head off when you take that first smoky, saline, chaud-froid bite. Desserts are just as expertly prepared -- any sort of upmarket pudding/custard jawn will finish you off with style (creme brulee, panna cotta, budino, you get where I'm going here.) Last but not least, service is friendly, elegant and uber-professional. They care.

text: St. Louis sucks for getting good shows and the Pageant is slightly a step above some of the corporate venues like the House of Blues, so I will give them that. This basically is like a crap version of the theater style venues like the Metro in Chicago. The Pageant isn't all bad, but its faults far outweigh its merits. Let's get the good over with first. The Pageant, once you actually get in and sit down, is not a bad place to see a large show. It's a good atmosphere when there's a packed house and in general the seating is comfortable. I don't really care to see shows in this way, but it is what it is and the sound system ain't bad. I've definitely heard better in theaters this size, but it's okay, definitely not a liability. Now, I don't mind some security, but getting into the Pageant is like getting into the airport. It's incredibly ridiculous, unnecessary, and over the top when it comes to security. I went there a couple weeks ago for the Explosions in the Sky show and you'd think it was Gangbanger Jamboree or something from the level of security at the place. I'm sure there's a LOT of kids going to the Explosions show packing, guys. After getting patted down, I was placed into one of two lines, the one for over 21's. Check the ID, get the special over 21 stamp. Okay, fine. But when I try to go upstairs, which is an over 21 area, I get ID'ed again!!! WTF, man, you just checked behind my ballsack and went over my ID with your special light to give me a SPECIAL STAMP which said I was over 21, why the hell are you ID'ing me again? To add insult to injury, they ID'ed me ONE MORE TIME when I tried to get an overpriced beer at the bar upstairs (yes, the bar in the restricted area). What the hell, guys, that is insane. And don't try and tell me you are just doing your job, you have to get by 15 dudes just to by a brew and that is too much work. Just make the venue 21 and over only if that's how ridiculous it has to be. Or don't sell alcohol at all ages shows, whatever. Just don't make it like trying to pass customs to get a drink. The upside is that the actual security guards and bouncers once you get past all the nonsense are actually quite pleasant most nights and pretty lenient for a hoity-toity venue like this. HOB bouncers are like Gestapo compared to these guys, so I don't really understand what people are complaining about there. What can I say, I moved up here from more of an industry town, but the calendar at the Pageant is below average at best. They have the same bands come through every few months and rarely get the killer tours to come through town. They need some better promoters, probably. If they would ease up on security (or at least streamline it) and get a better calendar, this could be a 4 star venue, but as is, it's pretty much a huge disappointment. Also, the attached Halo Bar is basically hipster hell and absolutely not recommended for any purpose.

text: this has to be said. the CUPCAKES at the flying monkey at the reading terminal are terrible. text: I'll be honest here, I'm extremely conflicted about how to rate this restaurant. If I was coming in to have drinks with friends it would be rated much higher. Their Margarita is phenomenal. So from that perspective it's well worth your visit. However, on my visit I was there to eat with my family. Let me get the positives out of the way first. I like the space a lot, the primary dining area is a little disjointed from the feel of the bar area but they both have their own solid vibe. The service was very attentive (maybe overly so), and I liked our server well enough. The chips, salsa, and guacamole were good. And their beans were very good. On to the negatives. The food was just mediocre. There was nothing I would describe as *bad*, just nothing that met my expectations. I had the Latitude which consists of Chile Relleno (not bad), Brisket Nachos (the Queso was fine, barely a piece of brisket to be found), and a Chicken Taco (completely flavorless). The table also had the beef fajitas, which had the grill been hotter to get a decent char on the meat would actually have been very good. Unfortunately without that you lose the bulk of the flavor you're looking for. It's not served on a sizzling platter, which I actually like because it means the meat doesn't end up completely overcooked, but some disagree. Lastly, there was a brisket burrito. Not bad, just not great. In general both the chicken and brisket were lacking moisture. This can happen late in the evening at many places depending upon how they are stored, but it was *very* early (around 5:30) so why this would be the case is beyond me. Mainly, I was disappointed because the elements are all there for a real winner. I like what I've seen of the people who run the place. I like what they're going for. But the flavor profiles and the preparations of some of the main dishes just didn't deliver. My hope is that it was just an off night, perhaps I will give it another try at some point and update. On a side note, there was a very cheap, decent looking option for those with children. You pick 2 out of 4 options and it comes with a drink for $4.95. 2 of the options were mexican (taco, quesadilla) and 2 were those old standby's for picky children (buttered noodles, fries) that their parents are appreciative of.

text: Maybe I am stuck in my ways with East Bay Area Vietnamese food but this place was an extreme disappointment. Maybe its just me, and you can argue that, but the famous soup here was a huge disappointment. The noodle is basically spaghetti and I was expecting the traditional thinly cut, transparent and chewy pho. I got nothing of that sort. Secondly, if you are not as accustomed to hardcore Asian dining (as I am not), the soup features an array of ingredients that may make you uneasy: pig feet, blood cubes, etc. Lastly, although claiming to be hot, this soup was not spicy at all and lacked any interesting flavor. The egg noodle was also very overcooked and the wontons were nothing special. Broth was plain and didn't do much for me. I give this restaurant a one star for the food, and another for the service. Although there was one stern lady working at the register and tables, we didn't get here and instead got a very pleasant woman who was extremely nice and polite. text: Strangely enough, I saw an episode of A&E's "Intervention" where a sort of sad and lonely guy came here to meet "friends" and no one showed up. So why not come here? We headed out to South Tucson tonight with the idea of finally trying Micha's, which I had wanted to try for a while. Problem is that Micha's is closed on Mondays. Oh well. Plenty of other places in South Tucson to try: why not Rigo's? Now, Rigo's is caddy-corner to one of my favorite places in the city, Crossroads Cafe, which is excessively cheap, has fantastic food and has one of the best chimichangas I've experienced (yeah, it was an experience). So I have to compare Rigo's to them, if only for the location. We came in and were quickly seated in a restaurant that was maybe 35% full. They had an awkward guy playing awkward keyboard music in the corner, who would stop every once in a while and make it even more awkward because no one would clap. Chips and salsa were brought out immediately, with two varieties: spicy and mild. The mild was full-on red, but the spicy had chunks of tomato, cilantro and onion in it. Spicy it was not, but the cilantro was nice. The mild was more like a fragrant ketchup. In all honesty, the taste was nice, it was just so non-spicy that I had a hard time with both of them. I ordered the "Muy Very Good," a carne asade chimi slopped in enchilada sauce, and served with lettuce and pico. My companion got a red chile burro with rice and beans. The food came out excessively fast. I mean, it was that sort of fast that makes you think that they already had it prepared and just slopped some of the sides and sauces on it. When it came to the red chile burro, it tasted like that too. The tortilla was really dry, the red chile sauce had no spice to it and very little flavor. The beef strangely got a little better as you moved into the center of the burrito, which made me think that it really had been sitting under a heat lamp for a while. I also have some experience with red chile burros at other places around town. I would say that, the majority of the time, Nico's is better, but I've had some at Viva that weren't as good. Although it completely depends on the Viva location. Now, of course, I'm comparing this "restaurant" burro with that of fast food but, if you justifiably compare to the red chile burros at some other actual restaurants in town that have it (Mosaic, Sanchez, El Charro, etc.), there's just no contest. My chimi was not awful, but, if I was somewhere that I knew had better food, and got this, I wouldn't get it again. The enchilada sauce slopped on there was definitely homemade (it didn't taste like that stuff you get out of the can) but there was nothing special about it: it didn't have any subtle flavor, no spice, nothing interesting. The chimi itself was that same sort of low-grade or old tortilla that was in my companion's burro, but the fried-ness sort of covered it up a bit more. The carne asada inside tasted more like fajita meat, in that it was grilled on a skillet instead of "asada" as the name implies. Honestly, I've had better carne at Los Betos. Maybe I've just gotten spoiled on Mexican food while living here, because I don't understand why you would eat here when there are so many better places in town. Like I said, try Crossroads, across the street. Prices: a little on the high side for Mexican. My dish was $9 and my companion's was $7.50. For what it was (not even considering that it kind of sucked), it wasn't worth it. Across the street, at Crossroads, the chimi I got runs for about $6. Although it doesn't come with that kick-ass shredded iceberg lettuce on the side. Service: not great. The waiter was nice, but he was a little slow and unattentive. He told us we could pay the check at the table but, after about five minutes of sitting there with the card on the table, we just took it up to the counter. I also asked for more chips at one point, he nodded in understanding, but they never came although, strangely, another bowl of the "spicy" salsa did. So why 2*? Well, the atmosphere was actually pretty nice, and the food wasn't necessarily bad. I've been home for an hour or so, and haven't gotten sick, which is definitely a good sign. I mean, I think if you're looking for a place to take, say, your 70-year-old grandmother from Michigan who thinks of "Mexican food" as On the Border or some other complete, disgusting garbage, then go for it. Because, then, yeah, it'll be an improvement. But go to other places on the south side, or even more in the city (hell, El Charro even beats this place, hands down) and it's just way, way better. There's just no reason for this.

text: I go here once or twice a month because it is pretty far away from my house. If I lived close by I would come every week. What a plethora of choices! The tapas alone are plentiful and varied; add dinners, soups, salads, paella... and you can eat here without ever getting bored. They always have a seasonal menu which is shared at the table and introduced by your server. There are also usually a couple of things that aren't on the menu at all that are special for the night. The dessert list is long and all of the desserts are house made, phenomenal! They have a great cocktail menu with some very unique choices. I don't know a lot about Spanish wines but they always recommend something that suites my palette and my meal. The owners are always there and everyone who works there is in good spirits. Live music is a nice touch. I almost always go on weeknights because I prefer the laid back and less busy atmosphere. Service has been rocky in the past but I have become familiar with the people who work Wed. and Thurs. (when I usually go) and they are great and attentive. I really can't say anything bad, but one thing I have learned about tapas though is that it is best to share, because the tapas are not served to the individuals who ordered them they are just placed on the table. If you want separate meals order dinners. As for the people who feel the prices are high, I don't know how you expect to get food of this quality and proportion at a lesser price! Not to mention the potatoes they bring to your table at no charge and never ending bread to sop up the delicious sauces. Here's what I recommend: anything from the seasonal menu especially the beef with cream sauce, the oso buco, and the cabrilla with artichokes! for the regular tapas: the cheese with grapes, the Spanish tortillas, the eggplant in wine sauce, the shrimp in wine sauce, the mushrooms with ham, the bechamel croquettes, the beer battered cod, the large scallops, and the scrambled eggs with shrimp and asparagus. The soups are all great and the steak dinner with mushrooms kicks ass. I have come here with people on restricted diets who have plenty to choose from, the vegan dinner with roasted almond sauce is yum, but not listed on the menu. I just love this place and we are so lucky to have a restaurant like this in Tucson of all places. Okay, maybe I just need to move downtown.

text: Going into Mostly Books always lulls me into a dreamlike state. The store is piled high with books and goes far back, and has the feel of someone's attic. It's one of those stores you can browse in forever. It is not for people looking for an organized, polished shopping experience. It's for people who like to rummage and don't mind getting a little dusty doing so. Most of the books are a couple dollars, and I've gotten some great stuff there- books about 1920's Paris, 1910's children's picture books, campy 70's novels. I also like their record selection, priced from about $2-10. It's usually full of those kind of basic records that are keystones to people's collections- you know, like Rumors and Blonde on Blonde. I got an album from The Move there that is definitely hard to find for $4. The trunk of old photos are 75 cents each or three for two dollars. They also have a very organized photo section with photos in plastic wrap that cost more like $2 each. Again, this could get pricey if you want to buy tons, but I don't think this is an unfair price at all when buying a cheesy new greeting card costs twice that (and using old photos to make your own birthday cards is way better.) I've also traded stuff here and they took everything, so it was fun to roam around with my credit slip and see what I could get. I think part of people's issue with the prices is that books, unfortunately, have become undervalued as so many bookstores close and fewer people read and there is stuff like amazon.com taking over, so people balk at paying $4 for a book even if that's the same price they paid for their morning latte.

text: This architectural landmark in Tucson has quite a twisted history...the fourth replacement for the original church of St. Augustín de Tucson (founded in 1776), construction began on the new cathedral in 1897 under the supervision of two French-born bishops (Salpointe and Bourgade), who envisioned a Gothic structure with two pointed spires (which were never completed due to lack of funds). For thirty years, the church stood unfinished, with bare-brick walls, until American-born Bishop Gercke decided to finish it in the Mexican baroque style. Inspired by the Mexican Catherdal of Querétaro, the sandstone façade and mission-style towers were completed in 1928. Structural deterioration prompted a restoration in 1966 under Bishop Green, who demolished everything except for the facade and the twin towers. The new building (completed in 1968) sadly is a product of its age...industrial acoustical tile, kitchy folk tapestries adorn the clerestory, a giant floating Jesus looms over the altar, red kitchen tile lines the floors and ceiling mounted florescent lamps cast a dull pallor over the interior. After the stunning entrance, quite a disappointment indeed...

The BF has hyped up the stadium so much (he grew up going to games, and a huge cardinals fan), and it's one of the few times there the hype lived up to itself. We got there little early, to check out the stadium. it was large, yet easy to get around in. The stores were awesome, people were so nice (those stereotypes about Midwesterners-- true), and helpful. The sea of red seats was overwhelming. It was beautiful. I think the success of creating a great stadium is a combination of easy navigation, nice service and people, cleanliness, how much of home can be emulated and the aura- the "love for the game" air you feel throughout the air. Everyone there seemed like true fans, and they acted respectfully to fans of the visiting teams. Very classy. This place embodied all that. And i got out a very memorable experience from the visit.

text: Huge disapointment. Some locals took me here to experience "The best or at least the most famous cheese steak is South Philly". I hope it is not the best because if it means trying anything worse I am done with the experience. As for it being most famous this is more likely as this place is lit up like a traveling carnival where you pay a ridiculous amount but still feel cheap after the experience. Geno's serves up three items: a steak sandwich with a choice of three cheeses, fries and sodas. So as specialists, one would expect something a little special. The steak is sliced, not chopped, flavorless and not seasoned. The sprinkled diced grilled onions added upon request don't add enough to the taste. If you want really bland go for the provolone, you won't notice it is there. Oddly the worst cheese ever, American, is a step up. Finally the whiz, probably not an actual cheese, provides the gooey messy textures one might expect but the combined flavors again are absent. $7+ for sandwich $4+ for small cup of cheese fries + soda = $15. to sit out side underneath a white neon canopy. While we were eating, the nearby insect zapper stayed busy and the bugs continued to meet an unsatisfying fate while I dined. I don't ever not finish my food. This once, I left a quarter of my sandwich not because I was full or bloated, but instead I was bored and lost my appetite while eating. If you have to go here, do not say "please" and/or "thank you" while placing your order. I was not pleased to fork out 15 bucks or thankful to have digested this bland "comfort food." Philly cheese steak, At least this Philly cheese steak is not a must have, must experience to appeciate the local flavor and culture type of thing... At least not this cheese steak.

text: I really wanted to have a good experience but alas, it wasn't so hot. We had lunch here a few weeks ago. It was the middle of the week around 2/2:30 and the place was empty. I was relieved because I always hear how busy it is on the weekends. The service was fine and so is the atmosphere/decor. I love the photos on the wall. So far so good... We ordered: The breakfast salad (aka Salad Lyonnaise) The flatbread white pizza (tomato, spinach, garlic & ricotta) Coffee Passion fruit soda "peanut butter" cookie The Salad Lyonnaise was good but not by any means one of the best I've had. Unfortunately the poached egg was way overcooked, leaving me with a solid egg yolk. This bums me out because if you're a lover of the lyonnaise salad, you know that breaking the yolk and mixing it into the salad is an integral part of dressing the salad. So without a yolk, there's wasn't as much flavor. They serve it rustic style, meaning bigger potatoes and bigger slabs of bacon, with huge hunks of fat on them as opposed to the more traditional cubed lardons. I'm not crazy about the huge hunks of fat they leave on the bacon although I appreciate the flavor they lend. I tend to lean more towards the traditional cubed and crisped lardons but hey, it's still bacon, and hey, I guess that's why they call it the breakfast salad instead of Salad Lyonnaise. Anyway, long story short; it was good but not great and certainly not one of the better ones I've had in the city. The white flat bread pizza was just...awful. Not only did it lack flavor but it was so dried out and hard as a rock. It tasted like it had sat out for hours, been heated, sat out again and the re-heated, and then served to my mother. My poor mom, I'm always excited to bring her to these places I hear great things about and she always ends up with the worst dish. Anyways, I wouldn't recommend it...at all. The passion fruit Italian soda I had was good but I probably should have ordered black cherry since I like the flavor better. Coffee was barely lukewarm. Our server was kind enough to heat it up for my mom. The decaf is not so great but the Sumatra had a good rich flavor. The Cookie: When I went to pay at the register I noticed some naughty looking cookies nearby. I spotted a big old peanut butter cookie with the mashed fork impressions in it and I immediately bought one and brought it back to the table. Christ, what a dick tease. That cookie tasted nothing like a peanut butter cookie. It tasted more like a cross between a snickerdoodle and a sugar cookie. blah. I dunno...maybe it wasn't peanut buttter flavored...? If it wasn't then it should be illegal to put those crossed fork impressions in them! I'm going to give this place a few more tries. It had to have been a fluke. But until then this cat gets 2 stars.

I had the chilled cucumber/avacado soup with spicy chili oil and shrimp. Perfect summer starter and one of the best soups I have ever had. She had a scallop appetizer that she seemed equally pleased with. For entrees I had the crispy red snapper and she had the "halibut in a potato nest'. text: US Post Office - Creve Coeur and the Main, Downtown St. Louis office. Ever have a problem with the US Post Office? What results did you get? Better than mine, I hope. Guess, again, if you think they care or if you'll get any help at all!. Shouldn't a 'Certified Letter, Return Receipt Requested' get special handling? I think so. It costs $5.54 rather than 44¢ to mail one. That's more than 12 times the rate of a first class stamp! I mailed a VERY IMPORTANT letter this way on March 31st. It has legal and high monetary implications, and was time sensitive. It NEVER got delivered. It NEVER got returned to me! (I had an slightly incorrect address, although I had the same incorrect address over a month earlier, and it did get delivered. It was the correct post office and zip code. NO Return receipt was sent to me.) NO ONE returned my calls at first. Customer Service didn't, the manager of the Creve Coeur Post Office didn't, the Postmaster General of St. Louis's Office didn't either. FINALLY, the manager of the Creve Coeur Post Office (after he had been conference called with me on Monday, the 12th) called late afternoon to confirm the letter was NOT DELIVERED and he DIDN'T HAVE A CLUE where it was! I asked who's responsibility it was and he replied. "I don't know." WOW! Don't lawyers and accountants suggest we mail important documents this way? In private industry, a customer service person who knows customer service and cares about customers, would have sent a courier to my house immediately to pick up and hand deliver the important document. Finally, after another call, they did pick up the letter, and, lo-and-behold! - Delivered it the same day. (I received the signed, return receipt card the next day, inside an envelope from the Creve Coeur Post Office. It's a shame it wasn't done correctly the first time.
label: NEG

And the furniture store, on top of having good deals on really beautiful pieces sometimes, has HILARIOUS price tags. text: The Fatted Calf is a pretty cool place to go. I went by there for lunch today and got one of their super duper hamburgers. Of course, being a big fan of not having the earth destroyed by not having a hamburger, I had one. I was glad that I had one too because it was terrific. The burger is nice and large, 1/3 pound of meat ready to be consumed for your eating pleasure and what a pleasure it was to eat it. Of course I also had cheese on my burger and when I say cheese, I mean lots of it. They are not shy about giving you cheese, oh no, they use and ice cream scoop to lop it on. The Fatted Calf is a great place to eat lunch and dinner, though I have only been there for lunch I would easily assume that dinner is just as good, only it is a little bit darker outside. The coleslaw contained black pepper. The problem with using this much black pepper is that your food ends up tasting like black pepper. The two pork products were expertly cooked so it was a shame that all one could taste was black pepper. The mac & cheese was good, but only if you like it really spicy. It was full of hot green peppers. The baked beans and buns were excellent. I want to go back to support a locally owned business, but someone in this place needs to please learn to diversify the spice blend used on the meat. I would suggest taste testing the rubs from places that have stood the test of time like Jim Neeley's Interstate BBQ, Corkeys, or Charles Vergo's Rendezvous.

text: I have always dreaded going to the hair salon. I hated the phony atmosphere of most places and I really dreaded the small talk I would be forced to have with my stylist. Andre is warm and personable and made me feel at ease immediately. Right off the bat, we connected on a topic I care about--dogs--and I didn't feel uncomfortable at all. Oh, and the cut and color were fantastic! My highlights last longer than highlights I have received from any other salon. For the past year or so, Christopher has been styling my hair and I LOVE him to death. He is incredibly sweet, down-to-earth and talented! My hair looks amazing for days after he styles it and, try as I might, I can never get it to look as good as he can. The last time I was at the salon, Christopher, Leah and I had a blast reminiscing about '80s fashion! I can't remember a time when I enjoyed going to the hair salon (which is probably because I never have!). Also, back in the spring, I asked Andre if he would be interested in donating a gift for a charity 5K I was helping to organize. Being the wonderful person he is, Andre didn't hesitate and put together a beautiful basket that was a hit at the race! Andre has a good heart and that it what I love about going to his salon! I also love that clients can schedule appointments online through schedulicity! Great prices, great cuts, great color, great space, convenient scheduling options and, most importantly, great people--you will not regret choosing Andre for your next cut or color!

text: Last weekend I had an incredible weekend in New Orleans with my family. It's walking distance from The Court of Two Sisters, Cafe du Monde, and many local shops I enjoyed browsing, including a wonderful knitting shop called the Quarter Stitch. Harrah's is a couple of blocks away and if you're not up for walking, there is a cab stand on the corner. Since this hotel encompasses an entire city block, it is home to a gift shop, a couple of restaurants including the lovely Begue's, as well as multiple bars. At the Mystick Den we saw an amazing jazz show featuring vocalist Betty Shirley. If she's playing, do not miss her. Dear families, I've heard that if you stay on a room that faces out to Bourbon Street on the weekends, it can be quite loud. We were lucky to get an inside room facing the courtyard and pool. Besides just pre-made meals, M & M also offers party packs. As the name suggests, this makes it easy to accommodate a lot of guests. Two that I would recommend are the Oriental pack- consisting of bite sized vegetable spring rolls, chicken breast, and boneless pork loin, and the Shrimp packs- sweet & spicy shrimp, curry shrimp samosas, ginger shrimp twists and sweet & sour wonton. This is the perfect finger food pack for any gathering. The staff are also very friendly and helpful. text: The Indiana State Fair is everything Indiana. From great unhealthy food to beautiful (and smelly, but what do you expect, it's August) farm animals, the Indiana State Fair has something for everyone. There's the State Band competition, concerts from the American Idol's finalists, food, games, rides, food, desserts, souvenirs, home made goods, (did I mention the food?), vendors, 4H competition, animal contests (including the pig calling contest), and most importantly, FOOOOOOOOOOD! There's waaaay too much variety to list, but here's a rundown of the itinerary developed over years of gastronomic study: First stop: The Other White Meat tent: Yes the pork tent serves up everything pork from tenderloins, to ribs, to the wonderful pulled pork barbecue sandwich. I always get the pulled pork. Second stop: Sweet Indiana corn dipped in melted butter and sprinkled with more butter. There is nothing other like it in the world... Third stop: Gotta get a Lemon-Shake-Up. Fancy shmancy lemonade, no sir! This is pure squeezed lemons, ice, a sugar/water syrup mixture shaken to pure-fection in yer cup! Now everyone: AAAAAHHHHH! Fourth stop: Can vary between a Dole Pineapple Whip, or perhaps a funnel cake, depending on the mood. Fifth stop: Indiana Rib-Eye tent around the bend by the Fall Creek Entrance and the antique barns. I always get a slice of cheese on this ribeye sandwich. Next walk around for a while on the north end of the fairgrounds to work off the overeating that just took place. Stop by the Chevy display to sit in a new Camero (or perhaps this year a Volt), see what other whacky attractions are going on (like year before last the Lombardi Trophy from the Indianapolis Colts Super Bowl XLI win, or last year's HP photo pavilion). Maybe this year do kiddie rides now that the little one is old enough to ride and would enjoy it. Next stop at the 4H building for the world's best strawberry shortcake (made the old fashioned country way!) Last, an elephant ear on the way out and a look at our new tans! (Budget at least $40 per person and $20 per person for rides, plus admission of $8 per person. Children under five are free) State fair here we come!

text: For lack of any better way to describe the dim sum at Wonton King, I'm just gonna say that this is the place that tastes "right." Now what the heck is that supposed to mean? To be honest that place is my favorite dim sum place (they've changed things up a lot in the past couple months) but some purists may say that it isn't quite right... Wonton King is probably as close you can get to the dim sum at the Chinatown in NYC, which was my first experience with dim sum and thus, is my de-facto standard for what's "right." They have all the standards and they're all tasty. The only thing that really stands out is the BBQ crispy pork that has a ridiculous thick layer of fat that is absolutely amazing. This is one of only a handful of other places in the area that serve this. However, because it can get crowded, you'll have to be aware of other offerings and let them know if you want them because chances are you won't see everything on their repertoire passing your table. Actually, you know what, forget about the dim sum. I actually like coming here on random weekdays for some congee or some wonton noodle soup. Sure, this is crap you can make at home easily, but you can make burgers at home too, but that doesn't keep me from going to McD's. When I'm tired, in a rush, or just need something light, yet filling, Wonton King is definitely up there on the list. Now why would I choose this place over Wei Hong or Mando House for this stuff despite the fact that they serve similar dishes? The TV. Sure, it may sound ridiculously stupid, but I don't like grabbing food for takeout, and if I just need a spot to unwind after a long day at work, looking at another couple hours of class ahead of me, I need a freaking TV, damnit.

(Though the people are a bit smaller, those free seats have their own speakers). The Muny is absolutely a St.Louis legend. It has seen some truly great performers on it's stage. The archives in the Muny (though a mess) holds an incredible amount of history. Back in the day, people got really decked out to sit in the stifling STL heat (and RAIN! some nights) to be here. The environment is magical. The actors (children, students and professionals) rehearse for 7 days before putting up the shows. The energy is palpable in the audience and backstage. For 2 hours, thousands of people forget where they are and fall in love with the theatre. There's nothing like it anywhere I've lived. Don't miss out when you visit. text: Two parts to this review, the station and Amtrak itself. Station: 1.5 stars. Amtrak Train travel in general: 3.5 stars. I really enjoy taking the train now. It is a new thing for me. Flying for years visiting relatives, although fun when I get there, is almost always torture. Squished together, the lines, check in, re-check in, security check, and now pat down/shoes off/power up laptop, take off jewelery etc.. ad nauseam... Amtrak has none of that nonsense. Advice: I always recommend the business class as it is only 20 bucks more, with the same lousy food naturally (hehe) but the seating is more spacious and comfortable with a lower noise volume which makes the comfort level goes up the scale to 100% in comparing to just regular fare. I have tried coach (LOUD and sometimes Greyhound-sque) & I have tried the lowest level of 2 person suite for travel (less leg room,) and I still prefer the business class. Perks: Business class you have 2 foot rests... one in front of you that you can rest your feet on and a leg/foot rest that props up like a lazyboy chair. You can lean back in your chair without disturbing who is behind you. There are 120V electrical plugs (for coach also) for every seat pairing. Pros/Cons: It is a longer way to travel, by train, but not that much longer if you are going to Chicago or Michigan. Sleeping our way to Michigan, rather then driving through the ice and snow is a blessing. Your luggage does not get searched, you can pack liquids and breakables as you choose, you don't have to take off your shoes, in business class you sit in a different (A LOT less crowded) waiting room. For $20 it is beyond worth the cost. Pros: Your luggage is always with you. You don't have to pack like someone might go through your stuff and you don't have to worry about your lip gloss causing an international incident etc.. If you pack something your big suitcase that is your favorite item, you don't have to worry about a luggage handler/sorter/etc.. lifting it off your hands. Carry that hair gel and in your carry on with no worries. This part is a big deal for me. Through many years of flying and the last few years of having to pack everything trying to keep in mind where to pack valuables (on me,) liquids of any sort (sealed in something and pray it doesn't burst in the suitcase.. oh the horrible memory of ruining a beautiful dress from Hair conditioner. :( etc....) .. THANK GOODNESS all I have to do is pack it up and go to take the train! Cons: Your luggage is always with you. Make sure ALL your luggage rolls or your shoulder bag is VERY light. Trust me. Your shoulders/back will NOT like you if you lug your heavy (or soon to feel that way) luggage around everywhere (thinking of Union Station and trading off to go to another hub.) The station itself: I like the location, as it seems a bit removed from the immediate area's traffic. The people who are working the ticket counter have 10 shades of attitude but they get 10 flavors of crazy going through there and not just mine. ;) (Good crazy is ok :p :D ) The fastfood joint is dirty and I couldn't bring myself to eat there. The chairs are horrible and there are no good places to put your luggage nor yourself for that matter. All sorts of characters walking in and out of there. I feel safe enough but I wouldn't have anyone I care about stay there too long waiting for me to pick them up. Always room for improvement. What's up: Take luggage that has wheels. Your shoulders/back/neck will scream at you if you try to carry bags everywhere. Pay the extra 20 bucks for business class for a much better experience. I love trains now. So stress free compared to driving/flying. Don't tarry at the station. Time your rides to be close to pick up time. I have heard many stories of VERY long waits for taxicabs, be warned. As you can call while you are on the train there is no reason to make people wait at the station for you or vise versa. Have fun! :)

text: There is peace in the gentle scrape slide of the pucks along the sanded court. Friday nights are different, though. The dollar admission becomes a requested donation, somebody hooks up their iPod to the sound system, and a broad spectrum of the St. Pete demographic turns out to play. Hip kids drink pouch wine and PBR from cups next to families out to explore or enjoy the friendly company. Dates are had - the game is conducive to conversation. text: Exquisite is the only word to describe the flavours that are produced and married in this beautiful restaurant. My aunt April and her boyfriend Steve were in town for the Greenday Concert so we decided to go for dinner. Khazana is just down the street from our condo so we decided to pop in for dinner as we are all big fans of Indian food. The restaurant was rather empty, but it was 5:30 on a Monday night. The lack of people was in our favor as we were seated right by the beautiful central firepit. The tables themselves are beautifully set with copper toned glasses and silverware. Our server quickly took our drink order and left us with an extensive menu to browse. He quickly returned with our drinks and told us about the "Special"- an array of appetizers and mains with dessert as well as a tour of the clay ovens and a demonstration on how they make Naan. We couldn't resist and it was a heck of a lot easier than trying to decide between four hungry people over a very large menu of delicious sounding delicacies! We were given a tour of the clay ovens and watched as the chef stuck and unstuck naan to the side of the ovens. The smell alone was worth the price of the "special". We then enjoyed the bread at our table with our meal. The food was beautiful and WAY too much for four people, as was to be expected for 40$/person. The curries were perfectly blended, the meat tender and juicy, and the saffron rice fragrant and subtle. We ate as much as we could and packaged the rest up. The left-overs fed my husband and I for three more meals! I will be back in the very near future for another sampling.
label: POS

text: Manny's has become a good standby bar for my friends and I- meaning a good catchall that most people can agree on. Gotta whole bunch people around and want to go out somewhere, anywhere, just for the hell of it? Why not Manny's? The main draw is the beer selection, one of the best on South Street. There are often specials for the economically challenged among us, but those in need of something significantly stronger than PBR will have nothing to complain about here. The food selection doesn't go beyond standard "bar food"- the difference is that they do it really well. I've always been a fan of the wings and nachos, my gf swears by the buffalo chicken. The back space is good for gatherings- I went there for my birthday this year and was very pleased. One of the best features is the surprisingly extensive jukebox selection, which allows me to impose my taste on unsuspecting patrons (Notorious BIG followed by Lisa Loeb- didn't see THAT coming, did ya!?). The TV selection is almost exclusively sports, for those interested. (I myself only enjoy the Olympics and the fair-weather Philadelphia teams).

The creamed spinach, hash browns and and (onions and chips) are best. The 16oz NY Strip, Bone-on 20oz New York strip or Colorado Lamb Chops are the best choices for meat eaters. text: Decided to walk in tonight since my friend who lives in the neighborhood has been raving about the selection of restaurants here. Things started out on a good note, we ordered, bread came with fruity olive oil. The bread would have tasted so much better if it were warm, but decent nonetheless. Before long we realized our entrees were taking a while, and I tried to flag down our server to get more bread. During the wait he never bothered to come over and check on us. When I finally got his attention, he came to our table and blurted out: I told you you should have ordered a salad or something because the food takes a while! I was quite taken aback by the attitude, and it took me a few seconds to recover and tell him all I wanted was more bread. A few minutes later, the food came: parpadelle with wild mushroom (good quality pasta, generous mushrooms), steak (very well-executed and seasoned, though the fennel in the fennel gratinata was waaaay too overpowering) and duck breast (good medium rare, thought it was sliced too thin though). The entree sizes were good for the price, and entrees brought to other tables looked equally enticing. At this point I was telling my friends: this place is worth coming back. Then....we got the check, and we instructed the waiter how to charge it onto two cards, but we forgot we're not supposed to add the tip to the charges, so the total on the two cards came out more than what's on the bill. Upon discovering this, the waiter looked all frustrated and came back to us and said very unfriendly: this total is more than the bill, what do you want me to do??? And he hands over a calculator and "ordered" us to figure out the remainder of the check to put on the 2nd credit card. I was simply stunned at the attitude. This isn't the first time we've included tip in the credit card charges, and most other servers simply charge the remainder of the bill on the other card and informed us about this. POLITELY. Any desire to return to this place has now fizzled. Apparently these people have no idea what service means.

text: I'm reviewing this place as a supper venue, not a brunch venue. And let me just say, it is exquisite. It's not usually too crowded for dinner. For those familiar with game theory, its like the El Farrol Bar problem: enough of a crowd so you don't feel like you're dining in a cemetery, but not so many to ruin your conversation. Additionally, their menu is seasonal and satisfying. Their portion sizes are perfect; I leave feeling satiated but not bloated. The best part about it is its BYOB status. They are not snobs. There is no corking fee, and you can bring in already opened bottles. This is ideal if you and your dinner partner don't feel like sloshing an entire pinot noir. The service has been good when I've visited. Timely, unobtrusive, but not write-home-about-it exceptional. My current menu item favorite is the pumpkin pie crème brûlée. Crunchy on top, creamy underneath, and delicious all around. Thus, if you are a native West Philadelphian, it's worth your time to check out Rx for dinner. Update: I went for dinner this month and had a less than thrilling gnocchi dish. While the gnocchi themselves were melty and mouth watering, they were paired with both corn and edamame. Not only was that too much starch, but those flavors are too similar for the combo to be appreciated. I think they need some more detail work with their vegetarian fare.

text: A great place to meet friends, have lunch, people watch, enjoy high quality food, shop for unique food items and soak up the relaxing and convivial atmosphere. We went whole hog at lunch today, meaning coffee, appetizer, main course and dessert. I thought the portions were just right for the ingredients and the price charged. I mean, we ended up needing a to-go box! I came into this deal knowing that the food would be a notch or five above the typical meat and three joint, and Marche fully met and even exceeded our expectations. The omelets and fried eggs were made from fresh eggs and were expertly cooked. The chorizo was tasty. The artisan cheese plate, now that was definitely way above average. The coffee was a unique, strong-flavored brew like Starbucks but better. The dessert display is beautiful, and the raspberry cheesecake tart split four ways was a great ending to the feast. The place was full when we got there, the waitress said expect to wait on the weekend. I am glad that Nashville has businesses like this one that pull together high quality food and food items that are from a variety of cultures. text: Do you know Al Merrick? Me neither, but the hand he's had in shaping (pun intended) modern surfing is known all over the world. If Kelly Slater and Rob Machado trust him, who am I to argue? My story: an impromptu surf trip to New Zealand lands in my lap a couple of weeks ago... YESSS!! Of course, I'll NEED (yeah, right - any excuse) a new board for sure. Something shorter, for ease of travel. Something that paddles easily, and catches anything - who knows what the waves'll be like in NZ? I didn't choose it, it chose me... Whatever. On their easily navigable website, I found a list of all the retailers that sell CI's boards, and called every shop from Australia to Honolulu to up and down the West Coast. Come to find out the Biscuit's a brand new model - no one's gonna see one 'til June. LAME! Out of desperation, I called the shop, and spoke with Kim: Alan G: Kim, I NEED a new Biscuit for my trip to NZ, and I'm leaving in like, ten days. Kim: Let me check... (pause) Hmm, it doesn't seem like we've shipped any out yet. I know we've got a whole bunch here though. Alan G: I KNOW that you haven't shipped any out yet - can you just send me one? Kim: No. We have an agreement with all our local shops not to sell direct from here. Alan G: (covering the phone) SHIT! (uncovering the phone) So, there's no way then, huh? Kim: Well, I suppose if your local shop doesn't have any Biscuits, (Didn't she just tell me that NO ONE had any?) and they didn't mind us selling you one, Scott, the shop manager, MIGHT send one to you. So after about 30 minutes of nicing-up my local shop owner, (Thanks Jeff!) I got permission, and called Scott. Alan G: Scott, I just spoke with Kim. She said I should ask you to send me a Biscuit. Scott: We don't do that. Alan G: I know, but Kim said you MIGHT make an exception if I got permission from my local seller, and told you how much I really, REALLY wanted it for my trip to NZ. Scott: Your local shop is cool with that? Alan G: Yes. Scott: What size do you want? You like Future fins or FCS? When do you need it? Alan G: 5'8". Future. NOW. Six days later, and I'm pleased as punch. Got it in the mail today!

text: This is a must-go location in Philly if you haven't been. I wouldn't come to Philly specifically for Independence Hall but it's still a worth while stop. It's the most important building in American history as well as one of the most picturesque spots in the city. In addition to the building itself the grounds (both in front and behind) are beautifully maintained and have plenty of open space. Unfortunately you can't just walk into the building and walk around at your leisure but it's extremely easy to walk into the visitors center get a free tour ticket and go over to the building and wait for the next tour to begin. The visitors center I've found is pretty boring and consists mostly of wordy plaques with lots of reading (and very few if any historical artifacts). Make sure to also visit the famous bell in the building adjacent to the visitors center, it's a little over-rated but it's free and it's a great part of history. The tour of the hall is very short but extremely informative and brings you into the two main rooms of the hall, the court room, and the meeting room where the Declaration of Independence was written. The rooms don't have a lot of original furniture but much attention has been paid to make both rooms as authentic as possible. It's a great experience to be in the space where the nation was practically born and then leave the building and stand in the back were the Declaration was first read to the people of Philadelphia.

When someone did take the time to hear me out they kindly informed me my mail was either thrown away or sent back as they don't keep mail that doesn't have a forwarding address. At the time I was working part time and got my checks through the mail. Since they stopped the mail my check (due to me that day) was returned. Additionally, the wedding responses, which should have been coming in, we were told were either returned or possibly discarded. At this point, I did become quite upset. My paycheck gone, my wedding responses lost and they keep telling me, "well you didn't provide a forwarding address and you didn't check your mail box daily." text: I want coffee, but I don't need to be stared at Through your thick glasses It's not you, it's me, Last Drop. Honestly. We've known each other since 2001. In college, we had some pretty good times. You were my go-to spot in the city during college, but my enjoyment started to ebb after a time. After moving to center city, I found plenty of other places not filled to bursting with snark and judgement. My love for you waned, and eventually you fell off my radar completely. Until moving back to the city in August of 2010, when to my horror I found you even worse. Let's back up just a second. Your space is great, and but for other factors would be a brilliant place to study, or even have some small acoustic shows downstairs. I love the old fixtures and shattered glass bathrooms, as well as the custom tile tables dotting the upstairs. You're quite a looker Last Drop, and not without your charm. The problem, I think, is that while your space is great, the same people who were there in 2001 are still there, only they didn't have a name back then. Nowadays we call them hipsters. Even your staff fits the mold to a T. The last time I was there I waited, patiently at first, for the girl behind your well-work counter to finish not one but two pages of her book before looking up to get me a lukewarm coffee from the urn. No and thank you for that sort of treatment and product. There's a second star here for the breads you carry; if I could order them directly and avoid the shop, I would. Like Christopher R. says, hit up Spruce Street Espresso instead. Better beverages and you won't have walk through a gauntlet of judgement. Sorry Last Drop. I promise I'll try to avoid the awkward eye contact when I walk by. We had some good times there but you're just not the same anymore. Actually you know what, never mind that first line. It is you Last Drop. It was you all along.
